documents/cutting-back-to-school-costs.m.text:
## Cutting Back-to-School Costs

School uniforms School lunches Rural school buses Buses, trains and fuel FAQs
Getting the kids ready for school will be more affordable under Labour with cheaper uniforms, healthy school lunches, rural school buses back on the road, and lower transport costs.

Key facts
- Cheaper uniforms: a law change limits the number of branded items schools can insist on, lets families buy cheaper alternatives from places like The Warehouse or Kmart, and requires schools to consider affordability. In place by Term 1 2028
- Healthy school lunches back from Term 1 2028: fresh and locally made, prepared in school kitchens, by iwi and hapū partners, or by local caterers
- Lunch funding: $5 per meal, and $6.50 for students in Years 9 to 13
- Rural school bus routes: national cancelled restored where possible, with a practical alternative where not
- Fare cap: $20 a week in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, $10 everywhere else, from 1 July 2027. Once the cap is reached, all remaining trips to and from school that week are free
- Fuel tax freeze: for three years

Every parent wants to give their kids the best start in life. But the cost of getting them to school keeps going up.

A secondary school uniform can cost as much as $1,000. Then there's the cost of school lunches, bus fares and petrol for the school run. For families already struggling with the cost of living, it all adds up.

Labour will take practical action to bring these costs down and make life easier for parents.

### Make school uniforms affordable

You shouldn't have to spend hundreds of dollars on expensive uniforms just to send your child to school.

Labour will change the law to:

- Limit the number of branded uniform items schools can insist parents buy
- Let families buy cheaper alternatives from places like The Warehouse or Kmart
- Require schools to consider what parents can afford when setting uniform rules
- Track uniform prices to make sure costs are coming down

Schools can still have their own colours and uniforms. But parents shouldn't be forced to buy expensive branded clothing when cheaper alternatives will do the job.

The new rules will be in place by the first term in 2028.

### Bring back healthy school lunches

National, ACT and New Zealand First took a school lunch programme that was working and made it worse.

Labour will bring back fresh, healthy, locally made school lunches from Term 1 2028.

Lunches will be prepared in school kitchens, by iwi and hapū partners, or by local caterers, with funding of $5 per meal and $6.50 for students in Years 9 to 13.

That means a decent lunch for kids, one less cost for parents, and more work for local food businesses.

### Bring back rural school buses

National has put extra costs on rural families by cutting school bus routes.

Many parents have been left driving further, spending more on petrol, or trying to find another way to get their kids to school.

Labour will work to restore the rural school bus routes National cancelled. Where that's no longer possible, we'll work with local communities to find a practical alternative.

Kids should be able to get to school safely, without parents having to spend a fortune getting them there.

### Cheaper buses and trains and a three-year fuel tax freeze

Parents shouldn't have to fork out hundreds of dollars a year just to get their kids to school by bus or train.

Labour will cap public transport fares at $20 a week in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and $10 everywhere else, from 1 July 2027.

Once you reach the weekly cap, the remaining trips to and from school that week will be free. That means cheaper travel for kids getting to school and parents getting to work.

And for families who rely on their cars, we won't add to the cost of filling up. Labour will freeze fuel tax for three years.

These are practical, common-sense changes that will make a real difference to family budgets.

### Part of Labour's Cost of Living Plan

Cutting back-to-school costs is part of Labour's wider plan to bring down the bills you face every week. See the full Cost of Living Plan for everything Labour will do on healthcare, power, transport and groceries.

Frequently asked questions
How will Labour make school uniforms more affordable?
Labour will change the law to:

- Limit the number of branded uniform items schools can insist parents buy
- Let families buy cheaper alternatives from places like The Warehouse or Kmart
- Require schools to consider what parents can afford when setting uniform rules
- Track uniform prices to make sure costs are coming down

Will schools still be able to have their own uniforms?
Yes. Schools can still have their own colours and uniforms. Labour's policy aims to reduce the pressure parents often feel to buy expensive branded clothing when cheaper alternatives will do the job.

When will these changes start?
- 1 July 2027: the public transport fare cap begins
- Term 1 2028: the new school uniform rules are in place, and fresh, healthy, locally made school lunches return
- Fuel tax: frozen for three years
- Rural school buses: Labour will work to restore the routes National cancelled, and where that is no longer possible will work with local communities to find a practical alternative

What will the school lunches be like, and how much will they be funded at?
Labour will bring back fresh, healthy, locally made school lunches from Term 1 2028. Lunches will be prepared in school kitchens, by iwi and hapū partners, or by local caterers, with funding of $5 per meal and $6.50 for students in Years 9 to 13.

Why is Labour bringing back school lunches?
National, ACT and New Zealand First took a school lunch programme that was working and made it worse. Bringing it back means a decent lunch for kids, one less cost for parents, and more work for local food businesses.

What is Labour doing about rural school buses?
National has put extra costs on rural families by cutting school bus routes, leaving many parents driving further, spending more on petrol, or looking for another way to get their kids to school. Labour will work to restore the rural school bus routes National cancelled, and where that is no longer possible will work with local communities to find a practical alternative.

How will the public transport fare cap help with getting to school?
From 1 July 2027, public transport fares will be capped at $20 a week in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and $10 a week everywhere else. Once you reach the weekly cap, the remaining trips to and from school that week will be free, making travel cheaper for kids getting to school and parents getting to work.

What is Labour's fuel tax freeze?
Labour will freeze fuel tax for three years, so families who rely on their cars won't face added costs when filling up.

How is this paid for?
Labour's election commitments are fully costed and fully funded, as set out in the independently reviewed Fiscal Plan. The public transport fare cap is funded by reprioritising 1% of the National Land Transport Fund, and the fuel tax freeze is fully funded within the Fiscal Plan.

How does this fit into Labour's wider cost of living plan?
Cutting back-to-school costs is part of Labour's Cost of Living Plan, which also includes three free GP visits a year, free prescriptions, solar with no upfront cost, a ban on price gouging, and action on hidden fees.

Cheaper uniforms. Better school lunches. School buses back on the road. Lower transport costs.

Better starts now.

documents/cutting-student-debt.md.title: Cutting Student Debt
documents/cutting-student-debt.md.text:
## Cutting Student Debt

What Labour will deliver How it will work Case studies Part of a bigger plan Fully funded FAQs
Labour will cut 10% off eligible student loan balances, so graduates who study, work and stay here can pay off their loans sooner, keep more of their pay, and get ahead at home.

Key facts
- Eligible student loan balances cut by 10%
- Already finished study and still repaying? Get the 10% cut on 1 April 2027
- Current or future student? Get the 10% cut after 3 years based in New Zealand following the end of your study
- Balances of $2,000 or less written off completely after the 3-year track
- Does not apply to graduates who benefited from Fees Free
- Repayments remain income-based, as under the current system
- Estimated cost: nearly $40 million a year once fully running, from 2031

Labour will cut student debt. If you've finished your study and you're still paying off a student loan, we'll wipe 10% off what you owe on 1 April 2027. And for every student who comes after, if you stay in New Zealand for three years after you finish your study, we'll also wipe 10% off what you owe.

Graduates will pay off their loans sooner, keep more of their pay, and get ahead here at home. Only with Labour. Better starts now.

Student debt can hang over people for years. It makes it harder to save for a home, start a family or plan for the future.

A Labour Government will make sure New Zealanders who study, work and contribute here can get ahead here. No one should have to move overseas to build a future.

### What Labour will deliver

- Cut student debt. On 1 April 2027, New Zealand-based borrowers who have finished their study will have 10% of their student loan written off.
- A 10% cut for people who stay. Current and future students who stay in New Zealand for three years after they finish study will also have 10% of their loan written off.
- Wipe off small balances. Graduates who owe $2,000 or less after three years will have their remaining debt written off completely.
- Reward people who meet their obligations. The 10% cut will apply to graduates who are up to date with their loan obligations and did not get Fees Free.
- Back graduates who build their future here. Cutting student debt by 10% for everyone who stays gives graduates a lasting reason to work and build their future in New Zealand.

### How it will work

#### If you've already finished study

If you've finished your study and are still paying off your loan, and you did not benefit from Fees Free, you'll get the 10% cut on 1 April 2027.

#### If you're a current or future student

- Finish your study and stay. Once you've finished your study, stay in New Zealand and keep up with your loan obligations for three years.
- Get the cut. After three years, we'll cut what you owe by 10%. Debt of $2,000 or less will be written off completely.

Student loan repayments will still be based on income. People who earn too little to make repayments can still qualify, as long as they are meeting their obligations. To be eligible, graduates must be New Zealand-based borrowers.

### Case studies

Each example assumes the person started study from 2025, stays in New Zealand for three years after graduating, and keeps up with their loan obligations, with the 10% applied to the balance still owed at that point. These examples are illustrative only. Actual outcomes will depend on individual salaries, pay progression, loan balances and any future changes to repayment settings.

#### A new graduate nurse

Tom starts a nursing degree in 2025 and begins his first nursing role in 2028 on about $77,000, with a student loan of just under $40,000. If he stays in New Zealand, under Labour's Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee, Labour will also write off 10% of what he still owes in 2031, around $2,000. Tom would finish repaying his loan sooner and keep more of his pay.

#### A first-year house officer

Mia starts her medical degree in 2025 and later begins work as a doctor on around $105,000, with a student loan of about $120,000. After three years working in New Zealand, she can expect around $9,000 of her loan to be written off. Mia can expect to be debt-free sooner under Labour and keep more of her pay.

#### A new teacher

Aroha starts a teaching degree in 2025 and begins teaching on about $66,000, with a loan of around $40,000. After three years in the classroom here, Labour will cut what she owes by 10%, around $2,400. She would finish repaying her loan sooner and keep more of her salary.

### Part of a bigger plan for young New Zealanders

Cutting student debt helps people get ahead once they're working. But young New Zealanders also need good jobs to go to.

Labour will guarantee a job offer for every new nurse trained here in New Zealand, so they can build their future while caring for people here. It means around 2,400 job offers every year.

We'll back small Kiwi businesses to grow and create jobs. And we'll get on with fixing schools and hospitals, creating steady work for local builders, sparkies, plumbers and the businesses that employ them.

Through the New Zealand Future Fund, we'll invest in Kiwi businesses so they can grow, expand and create jobs here at home.

Cutting student debt will help young people get ahead. Investing in jobs will give them a reason to build their future here.

### Fully funded, ready to start

Student loans sit on the government books as an asset. When Labour reduces a loan balance, the borrower owes less, and the government writes off some of that asset.

The value of the loan is not simply the total amount borrowers owe. Some loans won't be fully repaid, they're interest free, and repayments can take years. The true value of the loan is called the fair value of the loan, which is lower than the dollar value of the loan.

The first graduates will qualify under the three-year track in 2031, with an estimated cost to government of nearly $40 million a year once fully running. Labour will also fund Inland Revenue to make the change.

### Making life more affordable

Cutting student debt is part of Labour's wider plan to make life more affordable. Labour will also:

- Introduce new laws to make price gouging illegal
- Break the grip of the two supermarket giants so smaller stores have guaranteed access to wholesale and can offer fairer prices
- Provide three free GP visits a year
- Freeze fuel tax for three years
- Cap public transport fares at $20 a week in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and $10 a week elsewhere
- Make prescriptions free
- Help households install solar power with no upfront cost, saving around $1,000 a year

Frequently asked questions
How much will my student loan be cut by?
Eligible student loan balances will be cut by 10%. There are two ways to qualify: if you have already finished study and are still repaying your loan, you get the 10% cut on 1 April 2027. If you are a current or future student, you get the 10% cut after staying in New Zealand for three years following the end of your study.

Will my student loan be written off completely?
Graduates who owe $2,000 or less after completing three years in New Zealand following their study will have their remaining debt written off completely.

Who is eligible for the student loan cut?
To be eligible, you must be a New Zealand-based borrower who is up to date with your loan obligations, and you must not have benefited from Fees Free. People who have already finished study and are still repaying qualify for the cut on 1 April 2027. Current and future students qualify after staying in New Zealand for three years following the end of their study.

When do I get the cut if I'm a current or future student?
Current and future students receive the 10% cut after finishing their study, staying in New Zealand, and keeping up with their loan obligations for three years. Labour estimates the first graduates will qualify under this track in 2031.

Does the Fees Free exclusion apply to me?
The 10% cut applies to graduates who did not benefit from Fees Free tertiary funding. If you received Fees Free, you are not eligible for this reduction.

Do I still make repayments based on my income?
Yes. Student loan repayments will still be based on income. People who earn too little to make repayments can still qualify for the cut, as long as they are meeting their obligations.

How much could this save someone in practice?
These are illustrative examples only - actual outcomes depend on individual salaries, pay progression, loan balances and any future changes to repayment settings.

- A graduate nurse starting work in 2028 on about $77,000, with a loan of just under $40,000, could have around $2,000 written off after three years in New Zealand
- A doctor on around $105,000 with a $120,000 loan could have around $9,000 written off after three years
- A teacher on about $66,000 with a $40,000 loan could have around $2,400 written off after three years

How much will this cost, and how is it funded?
The policy will cost nearly $40 million a year once fully running, based on the fair value of the loan reductions rather than the full dollar amount owed, since not all loans would otherwise be fully repaid. Labour will also fund Inland Revenue to administer the change.

Why is Labour doing this?
Student debt can hang over people for years, making it harder to save for a home, start a family or plan for the future. Labour wants New Zealanders who study, work and contribute here to be able to get ahead here, rather than feeling they need to move overseas to build a future.

Owe less. Get ahead. Build your future here.

Better starts now.

### Teachers, ratios and pay

Labour will remove unnecessary barriers for qualified teachers, including working with Pacific and other centres where English is not the language of instruction on exemptions from English-language testing.

Labour is committed to genuine pay parity, working towards ECE teachers being paid fairly in line with other teachers.

Labour will strengthen oversight and transparency, with unannounced checks, clearer financial reporting and a better complaints process.

Labour is committed to genuine pay parity, working towards ECE teachers being paid fairly in line with other teachers.

Labour will give parents more choice and confidence, including better information about providers and support for a diverse range of high-quality early learning options.

Labour will restore ECE purpose as education, affirm Te Whāriki, and refresh the 10-year strategic plan to lift the quality of all forms of early childhood education.

## Labour's ED Recovery Plan

The problem Labour's plan Primary care Leadership More access FAQs
When someone you love needs emergency care, you should know they can get help quickly.

Key facts
- A four-part plan: make seeing a GP free, create more GP appointments and back local GPs; get more nurses into the health system; get patients through the emergency department (ED) and home or into a ward fasterr; and more care in the community
- Three free GP visits a year through the Medicard, saving the average household around $366 a year
- Free prescriptions. A New Zealand study found a 34% higher likelihood of hospital admission among people not collecting prescriptions; Labour says free prescriptions could help prevent around 27,000 avoidable ED admissions over three years
- Around 4.5 million more GP appointments a year by freeing GPs’ time through phone triage, better information for patients, and technology that reduces paperwork, backed by a new Digital Innovation Fund
- Up to 50 Family Doctor Loans a year, to support GPs to expand or set up clinics, capped at $500,000, from 1 July 2027
- Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee. Around 2,400 graduates a year offered work, with roles on graduation from 2027, and National's hiring freeze ended
- Clear direction from a Labour Minister at the first meeting with the Director-General of Health: an independent report on deaths linked to long ED waits, a nationwide stocktake of closed and unopened beds, winter planning restarted, and stronger reporting
- More care outside hospital: more extended-care paramedics (only 152 nationwide), a clinical telehealth service, longer emergency medicine supplies from pharmacists, and early supported discharge teams in every region

### When someone you love needs emergency care

Right now, emergency departments are overcrowded, patients are waiting too long, and doctors and nurses are under enormous pressure. Some patients are being treated in corridors because there is nowhere else for them to go.

Labour points to what is happening in hospitals around the country:

- At Starship, kids' cancer treatment has been delayed.
- At Tauranga Hospital, ED staff reported working at 150-200% capacity.
- North Shore nurses described days with three times the patients the department was staffed to care for.
- Wellington Hospital's ED was at code red for 84% of August.

National has stopped hospitals from hiring the staff they need. Over the past two years, Christopher Luxon's Government has added just 54 nurses to the public health system, while newly qualified nurses have struggled to find jobs.

+21%GP fees over the last three years

54Nurses added to the public health system in two years

650,000New Zealanders can't afford to see a GP or nurse practitioner

1 in 3People wait more than two weeks to see a GP

Far too many people can't afford an appointment or get one when they need it, leaving illnesses untreated until they turn into a trip to the ED.

Patients that need a hospital bed are often left waiting in ED because wards lack staffed beds. Others stay in hospital longer than necessary because support is not available at home.

Our healthcare staff are doing everything they can under huge pressure. But they're at breaking point and cannot keep being asked to do more with less.

### Labour's plan

Labour will act on each part of the problem:

- Make seeing a GP free, so people can get care before they need a trip to the hospital
- Create more GP appointments and back more local GPs
- Strong leadership from day one
- Making sure EDs are there when people need them, including getting more nurses into our health system
- Getting people the right care in the right place

### Our ED recovery plan starts with primary care

Making it cheaper to see a GP is essential. But free visits are only part of the answer. People also need an appointment when they are sick, and a local practice that can take them on. Regular care from the same GP helps prevent avoidable hospital admissions. Free prescriptions also help people get the medicine they need so their health doesn't get worse.

#### Three free GP visits a year

When money's tight, the cost of seeing a doctor is another bill many families struggle to afford. Around 650,000 New Zealanders can't afford to see a GP or nurse practitioner when they need to.

Labour will give every New Zealander three free GP visits a year through a new Medicard, saving the average household around $366 a year. This will put money back in families' pockets while helping people get checked and treated earlier.

#### Free prescriptions

Labour will make prescriptions free so that cost does not stop people collecting the medicines they need. Being able to collect medicines can help keep manageable conditions from becoming serious.

A New Zealand study found an association between not collecting prescriptions and a 34% higher likelihood of being admitted to hospital. Free prescriptions could help prevent around 27,000 avoidable admissions to ED over three years.

#### Free up around 4.5 million GP appointments a year

One in three people now waits more than two weeks to see a GP. Labour will help GPs make better use of clinical time and free up around 4.5 million appointments a year. We will support:

- Phone triage, so people are directed to the right care and appointments are available for those who need them.
- Better information for patients, so people have more help to manage long-term conditions.
- Technology that reduces paperwork, including AI tools, backed by a new Digital Innovation Fund.

These changes will give GPs more time with patients. More appointments mean people are less likely to go without treatment or turn to an overcrowded ED.

#### Back more local family doctors and clinics

Labour's Family Doctor Loan Scheme will help doctors open new clinics or expand existing ones where communities are struggling to get care, particularly where there is no GP clinic or practices have closed their books to new patients.

From 1 July 2027, up to 50 loans will be available each year, capped at $500,000, to help doctors buy into an owner-operated practice.

Free GP visits, free prescriptions, more appointments, and more local clinics will help people get care close to home, rather than going without treatment or ending up in ED because they had nowhere else to turn.

#### Prepare for winter before hospitals are overwhelmed

Winter illnesses put predictable pressure on hospitals. Labour will restore early winter planning on day one and bring together information from community health services, ambulances and hospitals to identify rising demand. Regular national and regional warnings will help services prepare staff and capacity before EDs are overwhelmed.

#### Put public health needs at the centre of vaccine decisions

Vaccines protect individuals and reduce the spread of illness across communities. They can also reduce the number of people who become seriously ill and need hospital care. Decisions about the national vaccine schedule should take account of those wider benefits.

Labour will put the Public Health Agency in charge of deciding the national vaccine schedule and who is eligible. We will direct it to keep the schedule up to date and ensure it meets New Zealand's health needs. Pharmac will continue to negotiate prices, supply and contract terms. This follows a recommendation from the 2022 Pharmac Review.

Free GP visits, free prescriptions, more appointments and more local clinics, and better planning will help people get care close to home, rather than going without treatment or ending up in ED because they had nowhere else to turn.

### Strong leadership

Overcrowded emergency departments have become the norm. Christopher Luxon and National have failed to treat it as the emergency it is. Long ED waits must be treated as a serious risk to patients, not simply a performance target.

At the first meeting between Labour's Minister of Health and the Director-General of Health, the Minister will set clear directions to begin addressing overcrowding immediately:

- Patient safety: order a rapid, independent report on deaths, quality and safety linked to long ED waits.
- Faster patient flow: require hospitals to use better real-time information and clear responsibility for decisions about moving patients safely from ED into wards.
- Available beds: carry out a nationwide stocktake of closed and unopened beds, the staff needed to open them, and other barriers to admitting patients.
- Winter readiness: restart winter planning immediately, rather than waiting for demand to surge.
- Clear accountability: strengthen reporting to the Minister and the public, including the Australasian College for Emergency Medicine's hospital access targets, and focus on patient safety and quality as well as ED wait times.

### Making sure EDs are there when Kiwis need them

#### More nurses and staffed hospital beds

It makes no sense to train nurses in New Zealand and then leave them struggling to find work when hospitals need more staff.

Labour's Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee will guarantee every eligible New Zealand-trained graduate nurse a job in our health system. Around 2,400 graduates a year will be offered work, with roles on graduation from 2027.

Jobs will be available in hospitals, primary care and community health services. We will double funding for graduate nursing roles in primary and community care, because when people can get care early they are less likely to end up in hospital.

Labour will also end National's hiring freeze immediately, so hospitals can recruit the staff they need, take pressure off existing nurses and care for patients sooner.

#### Open more hospital beds and move patients into wards faster

One of the biggest causes of overcrowding is patients waiting in ED after doctors have decided they need to be admitted to a ward. When a ward has no available staffed bed, those patients remain in ED, meaning there's less room for people who need emergency treatment.

Labour will identify unopened hospital beds and the staffing required to bring them into use. At Waitākere Hospital, for example, only 11 beds were opened in a new 30-bed facility. A nationwide stocktake will establish how widespread this problem is.

We will also tackle bottlenecks that delay admission or discharge, including ward staff shortages, limited weekend services and delays arranging support for patients who are well enough to leave. Better use of staffed beds means less time waiting in ED and faster care for people who need it.

#### Getting people the right care in the right place

Not everyone who needs urgent attention needs to go to hospital. With the right training and specialist support, more patients can be assessed and treated safely in their communities.

##### Train more extended-care paramedics

Extended-care paramedics have additional training to assess and treat people at home or at the scene, including providing medicines and treatment that can avoid an unnecessary trip to ED. There are currently only 152 nationwide. Labour will subsidise their training and improve training pathways so more paramedics can qualify.

##### Give health professionals access to specialist advice

Labour will establish a clinical telehealth service so paramedics, rural GPs, aged-care staff and other health professionals can consult an urgent-care or ED doctor. This will help them decide whether a patient can be treated safely where they are or needs hospital care.

The service will also support care when someone's usual GP or nurse is unavailable, including after hours, when calling an ambulance can otherwise become the default even for non-urgent problems.

##### Help people continue their regular medicines

Pharmacists can already provide an emergency supply of a patient's existing prescription medicine, but it is generally limited to 72 hours. That can be too short when someone cannot get a GP appointment, is travelling or needs medicine over a long holiday weekend.

Labour will review the rules to allow an emergency continuation of treatment beyond the current 72-hour limit. There will still be a maximum supply period and clear safeguards, including checking that the medicine is part of the patient's existing treatment. In government, we will also examine the cost patients face for emergency supplies.

#### Help older people recover at home and free up beds

Older people should be able to leave hospital as soon as they are ready, with the care and support they need to recover safely. Without that support, people can remain in hospital longer than necessary while other patients wait in ED for a bed.

Labour will fund early supported discharge teams in every region. These teams will provide short-term nursing, rehabilitation and practical support at home. They will help older people leave hospital sooner and can prevent some hospital admissions altogether.

### Better care before, during and after an emergency

When someone is sick, they should be able to see a family doctor without worrying about the cost or waiting weeks for an appointment.

When they need emergency care, there should be enough nurses, doctors and hospital beds to treat them quickly.

And when they are well enough to leave hospital, they should have the support to recover safely at home.

See Labour's full plan for affordable healthcare.

Labour's ED Recovery Plan is a package to reduce pressure on emergency departments (EDs) by acting on each part of the problem:

- Strong leadership from day one

National has stopped hospitals from hiring the staff they need, adding just 54 nurses to the public health system over two years while newly qualified nurses have struggled to find jobs, and GP fees have gone up 21% over the last three years, leaving illnesses untreated until they turn into a trip to the ED.

How will three free GP visits help with ED pressure?

How will free prescriptions help?

What is the Family Doctor Loan Scheme?
Labour's Family Doctor Loan Scheme will help doctors open new clinics or expand existing ones where communities are struggling to get care, particularly where there is no GP clinic or practices have closed their books to new patients.

From 1 July 2027, up to 50 loans a year will be available, capped at $500,000, to help doctors buy into an owner-operated practice.

How will Labour get more nurses into the health system?
Labour's Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee will guarantee every eligible New Zealand-trained graduate nurse a job in the health system.

Around 2,400 graduates a year will be offered work, with roles on graduation from 2027, in hospitals, primary care and community health services.

Labour will double funding for graduate nursing roles in primary and community care, and will end National's hiring freeze immediately so hospitals can recruit the staff they need.

What steps will Labour take to address ED overcrowding?
At the first meeting between a Labour Minister of Health and the Director-General of Health, the Minister will set clear directions to begin addressing overcrowding immediately:

- Require hospitals to use better real-time information and clear responsibility for moving patients safely from ED into wards
- Carry out a nationwide stocktake of closed and unopened beds and the staff needed to open them
- Restart winter planning immediately
- Strengthen reporting to the Minister and the public, including the Australasian College for Emergency Medicine's hospital access targets, with a focus on patient safety and quality as well as ED wait times

How will Labour get patients out of ED and into wards or home faster?
Labour will:

- Identify unopened hospital beds and the staffing needed to bring them into use (at Waitākere Hospital, for example, only 11 beds were opened in a new 30-bed facility)
- Tackle bottlenecks that delay admission or discharge such as ward staff shortages
- Limited weekend services and delays arranging support for patients well enough to leave
- Fund early supported discharge teams in every region to provide short-term nursing, rehabilitation and practical support at home for older people

What is Labour doing about paramedics and urgent care in the community?
Extended-care paramedics have additional training to assess and treat people at home or at the scene, which can avoid an unnecessary trip to ED, and there are currently only 152 nationwide.

Labour will subsidise their training and improve training pathways. Labour will also establish a clinical telehealth service so paramedics, rural GPs, aged-care staff and other health professionals can consult an urgent-care or ED doctor, including after hours, to help decide whether a patient can be treated safely where they are or needs hospital care.

What will change for emergency medicine supplies from pharmacists?

Labour will review the rules to allow an emergency continuation of treatment beyond the current 72-hour limit, with a maximum supply period and clear safeguards, including checking the medicine is part of the patient's existing treatment. How will Labour prepare hospitals for winter?

Who will decide the national vaccine schedule under Labour?

What will change for ED staff assessing and treating patients?
Labour will work with health services on practical changes to reduce delays in assessing and treating patients, including more testing at the point where care is provided.

How is the ED Recovery Plan paid for?
Every one of Labour's election commitments are fully costed and fully funded in its independently reviewed Fiscal Plan, which provides $15.5 billion of additional funding for health over the forecast period. This includes:

- Three free GP visits and free prescriptions funded through Labour's targeted capital gains tax, with every dollar raised invested in health
- The Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee costed at $525 million and funded from Vote Health cost-pressure funding
- The Family Doctor Loan Scheme, if fully subscribed, would loan out $25 million a year, with the cost to government being the forgone interest, estimated at less than $8 million a year.

When will these changes start?
- Immediately on taking office: National's hiring freeze ended, winter planning restored, and clear directions on ED overcrowding set at the first meeting between the Minister of Health and the Director-General of Health

## A Fair Go For Drivers

At the pump More competition At the mechanic At the car yard FAQs
Cheaper repairs. Fairer fuel prices. More choice. Owning and running a car is more expensive than it should be - Labour will take action.

Key facts
- Weekly fuel price reporting. The Commerce Commission will report every week on what fuel companies charge and what drivers pay
- Fuel price gouging banned. Fuel companies keeping prices unfairly high can be investigated and made to repay drivers
- Right to repair law for cars. Car makers must give local mechanics access to the information, software and tools they need
- Fairer deal for independent petrol stations, including spare NZTA land considered for new stations and EV chargers
- Secret car finance commissions banned, and 14 days to cancel add-on insurance without penalty

For most New Zealanders, a car is essential. You need it to get to work, do the shopping and get the kids to school. But too many people are paying more than they should to get where they need to go.

When fuel costs fall, the savings don't always reach the pump quickly enough. And car companies can limit your choice of mechanic by withholding the information needed to repair your car.

Kiwis hate being ripped off. Labour has already committed to banning price gouging and cracking down on hidden fees. We'll also tackle unfair fuel prices and give drivers more choice over repairs.

### At the pump

Everyone knows what it's like. The price of petrol shoots up, but takes ages to come back down.

International fuel costs go up and down. But we don't see the savings at the pump as quickly as we see the increases - and it happens all the time. A Commerce Commission report found that around 70 to 80% of cost increases are passed on in the first week, but only around 30% of decreases are. Labour will make that harder to get away with.

We'll require the Commerce Commission to report every week on what fuel companies are charging and what we're paying at the pump. When fuel costs fall, we should be able to see whether we're getting the savings.

And because Labour will make price gouging illegal, fuel companies that keep prices unfairly high can be investigated and made to pay the money back.

### More competition

Smaller independent petrol stations can help bring prices down. We'll give them a fairer chance to compete by:

- Strengthening rules so smaller retailers get fairer supply contracts
- Cracking down on terms that make it harder for them to switch suppliers or compete on price
- Requiring NZTA to consider whether spare land could be used for independent unmanned petrol stations or EV chargers

The Commerce Commission has found local fuel prices can fall by around 3 cents a litre when an unmanned independent station opens nearby.

### At the mechanic

When your car needs fixing, you want to take it to someone you trust and get it sorted without a huge bill.

But even a mechanic you've used for years can be unable to help if the car company won't share the software or repair information they need. You can end up having to go back to the dealer and paying more than you should. You should be able to choose who fixes your car.

Labour will introduce a right to repair law, starting with cars. Car makers will have to give local mechanics access to the information, software and tools they need to do the job. That gives you more places to go for repairs, helps keep costs down and means more work for local mechanics.

The Commerce Commission will be required to make sure car makers follow the rules, so they can't shut local mechanics out or charge them unfair fees for access.

### At the car yard

Buying a car is expensive enough without hidden catches. Labour will:

- Ban secret finance commissions that can push up the interest rate you pay
- Give you 14 days to cancel add-on insurance without penalty
- Make sure costs are clearer from the start

The price you pay should be clear from the start.

These protections sit alongside the car-buying rules in Labour's wider Fair Go Law.

### Labour will get on with it

These are practical changes to help make everyday life a bit cheaper and easier. They're steps in Labour's wider cost of living plan, which includes cracking down on price gouging and hidden fees, freezing fuel tax, taking on the supermarket giants and cutting household bills.

National promised to fix the cost of living. They made it worse. They've spent too long asking people to wait for things to get better. Labour will get on with it.

Frequently asked questions
Why do fuel prices go up faster than they come down?
A Commerce Commission report found that around 70 to 80% of international fuel cost increases are passed on to drivers within the first week, but only around 30% of cost decreases are passed on in the same timeframe.

How will Labour make fuel pricing fairer?
Labour will require the Commerce Commission to report every week on what fuel companies are charging and what drivers are paying at the pump, so it's clear whether savings from falling international costs are being passed on. Fuel companies that keep prices unfairly high can also be investigated and made to repay customers under Labour's separate Banning Price Gouging policy.

What is Labour's 'Right to Repair' law?
Labour will introduce a right to repair law, starting with cars. Car makers will have to give local mechanics access to the information, software and tools they need to repair vehicles, rather than forcing owners back to the dealer. The Commerce Commission will be required to enforce the rules, so car makers can't shut local mechanics out or charge them unfair fees for access.

How will Labour support independent petrol stations?
Labour will strengthen rules so smaller fuel retailers get fairer supply contracts, crack down on terms that make it harder for them to switch suppliers or compete on price, and require NZTA to consider whether spare land could be used for independent unmanned petrol stations or EV chargers. The Commerce Commission has found local fuel prices can fall by around 3 cents a litre when an unmanned independent station opens nearby.

What changes when I buy a car?
Labour will ban secret finance commissions that can push up the interest rate a buyer pays, give buyers 14 days to cancel add-on insurance without penalty, and make sure costs are clearer from the start.

What other cost of living policies has Labour announced?
A Fair Go For Drivers sits alongside Labour's wider cost of living plan:

- Fairer grocery prices
- Banning price gouging
- The Fair Go Law covering hidden fees and junk insurance (including similar car finance and insurance protections)
- Freezing the fuel tax for three years
- $20 Fare Cap in the major cities, and $10 for the rest of the country
- 3 free GP visits per year for every New Zealander
- Free prescriptions at every pharmacy
- Solar power with no upfront cost
- Cutting 10% off student debt

A fair go for Kiwi drivers.

Better starts now.

documents/fair-go-for-families.md.text:
## A Fair Go For Families

What Labour will do Why it matters Labour's plan to lower bills FAQs
No hidden fees. No traps. No rip-offs. A Labour Government will ban hidden fees, so the price you see is the price you pay.

Key facts
- Cars - junk insurance banned, secret commissions banned, 14 days to cancel car-yard insurance
- Whiteware and electronics - no checkout pressure-selling of warranties, prices shown upfront
- Phones and internet - full price shown upfront, easy online cancellation, no unfair exit fees
- Subscriptions - cancelling as easy as signing up, clear pricing on introductory offers
- Tickets - advertised price must include all mandatory fees, no surprise checkout charges
- Gyms - cancelling as easy as joining, no excessive notice periods or inflated penalty fees

This election is about the cost of living. New Zealanders are working hard and every dollar counts. A Labour Government will ban hidden fees, so the price you see is the price you pay.

Most New Zealanders will know what it's like to get to the checkout and find the price has gone up because of extra fees. Or to sign up for a subscription in a few clicks, then spend ages trying to cancel it.

You might have been pressured to buy an extended warranty, or paid for insurance only to find it doesn't cover you when something goes wrong. An introductory deal that might have turned into a much bigger price before you realised.

These tricks cost people money they can't afford to waste. You deserve to know the real price, get what you paid for, and be able to leave when a deal no longer works for you.

As part of Labour's Action on Bills, we'll introduce a Fair Go Law to stop businesses making money by tricking their customers.

### What Labour will do

The Fair Go Law will tackle hidden charges, insurance that provides little protection, and contracts that keep people paying after they want to leave.

#### Cars

- Ban junk insurance, including paint insurance and mechanical breakdown cover that excludes almost everything that could break down
- Require car sellers to show the total cost over the life of the agreement before customers sign up for a car sold with credit or insurance
- Ban secret commissions on insurance, including flex commissions that allow car dealers to increase a customer's loan interest rate in exchange for a bigger commission
- Give customers 14 days to cancel insurance bought at the car yard without any penalty

#### Whiteware and electronics

- Stop retailers putting pressure on customers to buy insurance and extended warranties at the checkout - these products will have to be sold the following day or over the phone
- Require prices upfront - for purchases on credit, show the total cost over the life of the agreement before customers sign up
- Strengthen warranty rules so the cover provides real value and the terms are clear

#### Phones and internet

- Show the full price upfront and make it easy to cancel or switch providers online
- Ban unfair exit fees, excessive notice periods and unclear automatic renewals that lock customers in and make switching hard

#### Subscriptions

- Make cancelling as easy as signing up, including online cancellation for services such as food boxes and streaming TV
- Crack down on unclear automatic renewals, unfair exit fees and excessive notice periods
- Clearly state when an introductory offer ends, what the ongoing price will be, and when customers will be charged

#### Tickets

- Require the advertised ticket price to include all unavoidable booking, processing and other charges - no more extra mandatory fees added as you go through the checkout
- Ban misleading discounts that leave out mandatory fees

#### Gyms

- Make cancelling as easy as joining, including the ability to cancel online
- Ban excessive notice periods, inflated penalty charges such as lost key tag fees, and unfair contract terms that keep people paying after they want to leave

### Why it matters

When you're trying to manage household bills, every unexpected fee makes it harder. A subscription you can't cancel means less money for groceries. Insurance that doesn't cover a necessary repair can leave you with a bill you thought you had covered.

Getting a fair deal shouldn't depend on spotting every extra cost in the fine print or having the time to chase a company until it lets you leave.

Labour's Fair Go Law will help people keep more of their money and make it easier to choose a better deal.

### Labour's plan to lower bills

Labour’s Fair Go Law is part of our plan to lower costs. A Labour Government will also:

- Make price gouging illegal, take on the supermarket giants so smaller stores have guaranteed access to wholesale and can offer fairer prices.
- Provide three free GP visits a year and make prescriptions free.
- Freeze fuel tax for three years and cap public transport fares at $20 a week in our main cities and $10 elsewhere, saving the average commuter $25 a week.
- Help families install solar with no upfront cost, saving around $1,000 a year.

Frequently asked questions
What is Labour's Fair Go Law?
The Fair Go Law is Labour's plan to stop businesses making money by tricking their customers, tackling hidden charges, insurance that provides little protection, and contracts that keep people paying after they want to leave. It covers cars, whiteware and electronics, phones and internet, subscriptions, tickets, and gyms.

What changes for buying a car?
Labour will ban junk insurance such as paint insurance and mechanical breakdown cover that excludes almost everything that could break down, require car sellers to show the total cost over the life of any credit or insurance agreement before customers sign up, ban secret commissions on insurance including flex commissions, and give customers 14 days to cancel insurance bought at the car yard without penalty.

What changes for subscriptions like streaming and food boxes?
Cancelling will have to be as easy as signing up, including online cancellation for services such as food boxes and streaming TV. Labour will crack down on unclear automatic renewals, unfair exit fees and excessive notice periods, and require companies to clearly state when an introductory offer ends, what the ongoing price will be, and when customers will be charged.

What changes for gym memberships?
Cancelling a gym membership will have to be as easy as joining, including the ability to cancel online. Labour will ban excessive notice periods, inflated penalty charges such as lost key tag fees, and unfair contract terms that keep people paying after they want to leave.

What changes for buying event tickets?
The advertised ticket price will have to include all unavoidable booking, processing and other charges, so no extra mandatory fees are added at checkout. Labour will also ban misleading discounts that leave out mandatory fees.

What changes for phone and internet contracts?
Providers will have to show the full price upfront and make it easy to cancel or switch providers online. Labour will ban unfair exit fees, excessive notice periods and unclear automatic renewals that lock customers in and make switching hard.

What changes for buying whiteware and electronics?
Retailers will no longer be able to pressure customers into buying insurance and extended warranties at the checkout - these will have to be sold the following day or over the phone instead. For purchases on credit, the total cost over the life of the agreement must be shown upfront, and warranty rules will be strengthened so cover provides real value with clear terms.

How does this relate to Labour's other cost of living policies?
The Fair Go Law is part of Labour's wider Action on Bills plan, alongside making price gouging illegal, fairer grocery prices, three free GP visits a year, free prescriptions, a fuel tax freeze, the $20 public transport fare cap, and SolarSaver.

Kiwis deserve a fair go.

Better starts now.

## Fairer Grocery Prices

What's not working What we'll deliver How we'll do it Who it applies to FAQs
More competition. More choice. Fairer prices. Labour will take tough action on the supermarket giants to get you a better deal at the checkout.

Key facts
- Two big groups, Woolworths and Foodstuffs, control more than 80% of New Zealand's grocery market
- Two new independently run wholesalers will be created: Foodstuffs Wholesale and Woolworths Wholesale
- Unfair contracts will be ended, so individual stores can lower prices, switch chains, or go independent
- Junk fees banned on food producers and suppliers
- Smaller supermarkets get guaranteed access to wholesale supply, which cannot be cut off as they grow
- Applies only to Woolworths and the two Foodstuffs cooperatives, not local dairies, cafes or independent grocers

New Zealanders are paying too much for groceries.

Labour will take action to increase competition, giving consumers more choice and fairer prices.

This election is about the cost of living and who will take real action to get it under control. We all know families are paying too much for groceries. Labour has a plan to make sure all Kiwis can get a fairer price at the checkout.

A Labour Government will also crack down on big companies ripping you off by making price gouging illegal.

This election Labour's offering real action to tackle grocery prices. After three years of big talk and inaction, National is offering another review.

### What's not working

New Zealand has lots of supermarket brands, but most are owned by just two companies: Woolworths and Foodstuffs. Together, they control more than 80 percent of the grocery market.

These two companies also control much of the wholesale supply that smaller grocers need to stock their shelves. That means a new or independent grocer often has to buy their products from the same supermarket group it is trying to compete with.

The big supermarket companies give their own stores better prices and better access to products. This often means smaller shops and independent supermarkets end up paying more, making it harder for them to compete and offer you a better deal.

Unless we tackle this problem, lower prices won't flow through to the checkout. New Zealand's grocery market is closed to protect the two big companies and lock out competition. Less competition means less choice and higher prices at the checkout.

National promised to fix the cost of living and bring grocery prices down. Since National took office, grocery prices have risen sharply:

- Butter is up 72%
- Bread is up 66%
- Milk is up 33%
- Beef mince is up 36%
- Cheese is up 31%

Despite talking big, National has had three years and done nothing. Now, with the election only weeks away, they say what we need is another review. New Zealanders can't eat a review. It's time for real action.

And Labour will act. We will open the market so more supermarkets can offer lower prices, giving shoppers more choice and a better deal at the checkout.

### What Labour will deliver

#### Better prices for shoppers

More grocers competing for your business will mean fairer grocery prices that last.

#### A better deal for small, independent supermarkets

Every supermarket and grocer will be able to buy products on better terms.

#### More choice at the checkout

It'll be easier for new supermarkets to open and for independent grocers to grow.

#### A better deal for food producers

We'll stop big supermarkets charging suppliers unfair fees when they receive nothing in return.

### How we'll do it

A Labour Government will deliver fairer grocery prices. Our first step to break up the supermarkets will be to free small grocers from anti-competitive restraints that keep prices high.

- End unfair contracts. We will remove the rules that stop individual stores, like Four Squares, lowering their prices, switching to another chain, or going independent.
- Ban junk fees. We will stop the big supermarkets charging food producers unfair fees for things that provide no real value to them, and that make pricing needlessly complicated.
- Back small supermarkets to grow and compete on price. Smaller stores will have guaranteed access to wholesale products. The big supermarket companies will not be allowed to cut off their supply when they begin gaining customers.
- Make payments simpler and fairer. We will simplify supermarket rebates and data charges so suppliers know what they are paying and what they receive in return.
- Start creating independent wholesalers. Woolworths and Foodstuffs will have to begin separating their wholesale supply businesses from their supermarket stores.

These steps will help smaller grocers compete and offer better prices, helping to build a genuinely competitive grocery market for the future.

Instead of the two supermarket companies controlling the market and shutting out smaller retailers, a Labour Government will create two independently run wholesalers: Foodstuffs Wholesale and Woolworths Wholesale. This will give smaller grocers more places to buy their products and make it easier for new supermarkets to open and grow.

We will know the plan is working when homegrown grocery chains are gaining market share, challenging the two big supermarket groups and offering shoppers a genuinely better price.

### Who it applies to

These new rules will apply to Woolworths and the two Foodstuffs cooperatives. They will not apply to local dairies, cafes or independent grocers. The changes are designed to help smaller businesses compete and offer shoppers a better deal.

### Better starts now with fairer prices for the future

Tackling the cost of living means finding long-term solutions to the drivers of high costs, but families also need a fair go now. That's why Labour will take immediate action to get the cost of living under control:

- Cap public transport fares at $20 a week in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and $10 elsewhere
- Provide three free GP visits every year
- Make prescriptions free
- Lower bills by helping households install solar power with no upfront cost, saving around $1,000 a year
- Freezing fuel tax for three years

These changes will put money back in people's pockets now. Our grocery plan will deliver lasting change by giving shoppers more choice and ensuring fairer prices that last.

Frequently asked questions
Why are grocery prices so high in New Zealand?
New Zealand's grocery market is dominated by two groups, Woolworths and Foodstuffs, which together control more than 80 percent of the grocery market and much of the wholesale supply smaller grocers rely on. A new or independent grocer often has to buy products from the same supermarket group it is trying to compete with, and the big companies give their own stores better prices and access, making it harder for smaller shops to compete.

How much have grocery prices risen under National?
Since National took office, the price of bread has gone up 66%, butter 72%, beef mince 36%, cheese 31% and milk 33%. A basic basket of essentials has gone up in price by around 27% in three years. If you were spending $300 a week on groceries in 2023, you're now spending $381.

What will Labour actually do to bring grocery prices down?
- End unfair contracts that stop individual stores lowering their prices, switching chains, or going independent
- Ban junk fees charged to food producers
- Guarantee smaller supermarkets access to wholesale supply
- Simplify supermarket rebates and data charges
- Require Woolworths and Foodstuffs to begin separating their wholesale supply businesses from their supermarket stores

What are Foodstuffs Wholesale and Woolworths Wholesale?
Labour will create two independently run wholesalers, Foodstuffs Wholesale and Woolworths Wholesale, separated from Woolworths and Foodstuffs' supermarket stores. This will give smaller grocers more places to buy their products and make it easier for new supermarkets to open and grow.

Which companies will these rules apply to?
These rules will apply to Woolworths and Foodstuffs. They will not apply to local dairies, cafes or independent grocers. The changes are designed to help smaller businesses compete and offer shoppers a better deal.

How will this help food producers and suppliers?
Labour will stop big supermarkets charging food producers unfair fees for things that provide no real value to them, and will simplify supermarket rebates and data charges so suppliers know exactly what they are paying and what they receive in return.

How will we know if this policy is working?
Labour says the plan is working when homegrown grocery chains are gaining market share, genuinely challenging the two big supermarket groups, and offering shoppers a better price.

How does this relate to Labour's Banning Price Gouging policy?
Fairer Grocery Prices tackles the underlying lack of competition in the grocery market. Labour's separate Banning Price Gouging policy makes it illegal for large companies with market power, including supermarkets, to charge unfair and excessive prices for essentials, with the Commerce Commission able to investigate and order repayment to consumers.

Fairer grocery prices for the future.

Better starts now.

## Fairer Workplaces

Labour will roll back the current Government's employment changes and restore a worker-centred framework.

Key facts
- Pay equity legislation restored in the first 100 days, with an immediate pay rise for 65,000 care and support workers
- Living Wage required for all directly employed workers of government departments and departmental agencies, and at least the Living Wage across the public service and publicly owned organisations
- Fair Pay Agreements legislation introduced in the first 100 days
- Collective agreements the default, with the choice of an individual agreement
- Leave entitlements reinstated that were removed by Holidays Act changes
- Most non-compete clauses banned, and existing terms and conditions protected when a business is sold or a contract changes hands
- Safer workplaces: National's health and safety changes reversed, a new offence of corporate homicide, and ILO Convention 190 ratified

### Pay equity and the Living Wage

Labour will restore pay equity legislation in its first 100 days and give an immediate pay rise to 65,000 care and support workers.

Labour will require the Living Wage to be paid to all directly employed workers of government departments and departmental agencies, and ensure the procurement standards are protected.

Labour will pay at least the Living Wage across the public service and publicly owned organisations, and work towards extending it across the wider public sector, starting with schools and hospitals.

Labour will also require employers to publish the pay gaps between different groups of their staff.

### Bargaining and job security

Labour will introduce legislation for Fair Pay Agreements in its first 100 days.

Labour will make collective agreements the default, while allowing people to choose an individual agreement.

Labour will review the Employment Relations Act, including minimum compensation redundancy provisions, so that:

- People are better supported when they lose their job
- Unions and employers can work constructively with the government
- Workers can bargain with whoever actually controls their work

Labour will protect people's existing terms and conditions when a business is sold or a contract changes hands, and ban most non-compete clauses in employment agreements.

### Leave and gig work

Labour will roll back the current Government's employment changes and restore a worker-centred framework that ensures fair pay, safe workplaces and decent leave.

Labour will reinstate leave entitlements that were removed by Holidays Act changes.

Labour will reject the gateway test and work on greater protections for gig and platform workers. Labour will also work towards ratification of ILO Convention 193, which provides international protections for gig and platform workers.

### Safe workplaces

Labour will reverse National's changes to health and safety law and strengthen protections at work.

Labour will create an offence of corporate homicide, and ratify ILO Convention 190 on violence and harassment at work.

Read about Labour's wider plan for good jobs →

Frequently asked questions

Labour will roll back the current Government's employment changes and restore a worker-centred framework that ensures fair pay, safe workplaces and decent leave. Labour will pay at least the Living Wage across the public service and publicly owned organisations, and work towards extending it across the wider public sector, starting with schools and hospitals.

Will employers have to publish pay gaps?
Labour will require employers to publish the pay gaps between different groups of their staff.

Will Labour bring back Fair Pay Agreements?
Labour will introduce legislation for Fair Pay Agreements in its first 100 days.

What will happen to collective and individual agreements?
Labour will make collective agreements the default, while allowing people to choose an individual agreement.

Labour will review the Employment Relations Act, including minimum compensation redundancy provisions, so people are better supported when they lose their job, unions and employers can work constructively with the government, and workers can bargain with whoever actually controls their work.

What happens to my terms and conditions if my employer's business is sold?
Labour will protect people's existing terms and conditions when a business is sold or a contract changes hands.

Labour will reject the gateway test and work on greater protections for gig and platform workers. Labour will also work towards ratification of ILO Convention 193, which provides international protections for gig and platform workers.

Labour will reverse National's changes to health and safety law and strengthen protections at work. Labour will also create an offence of corporate homicide and ratify ILO Convention 190 on violence and harassment at work.

documents/familydoctorloanscheme.md.title: Labour's Family Doctor Loan Scheme
documents/familydoctorloanscheme.md.text:
## Backing Your Family Doctor

Labour's Family Doctor Loan Scheme will free up more than 4.5 million GP appointments a year and give every New Zealander three free doctor's visits through the new Medicard.

Key facts
- Loans of up to 90% of the cost of buying into a practice, capped at $500,000
- Interest-free for the first two years; a 3% annual interest rate applies after that on the outstanding balance
- 10 years in total to repay
- Up to 50 loans available every year, prioritising areas with no GP or with closed or partially closed books
- Only available for owner-operated general practices, not corporate-owned practices - one loan per doctor
- Available from 1 July 2027, delivered through the existing Small Business Cashflow Loan Scheme
- Aims to free up more than 4.5 million GP appointments a year nationwide

### A Labour Government will

- Make doctor's visits affordable for all New Zealanders, with three free doctor's visits a year through a new Medicard
- Support more doctors to set up new, community-based practices
- Free up 4.5 million appointments a year so people can get an appointment sooner
- Fix general practice's long-term funding challenges

### How the Family Doctor Loan Scheme works

The Family Doctor Loan Scheme is a practical, targeted way to boost the number of clinics across New Zealand - and strengthen the ones we already have.

- Doctors can apply for loans of up to 90% of the cost of buying into a practice, capped at $500,000.
- The loan is only available for owner-operated general practices to ensure the scheme backs locally run GP clinics that stay closely connected to their communities.
- The loan is interest-free for the first two years. After that, monthly repayments begin on the outstanding balance, with an annual interest rate of 3 percent applying from that point.
- Doctors have 10 years in total to repay the loan.
- Up to 50 loans will be available each year, targeted to communities with no GP clinic or where GP books are partially or fully closed.
- Each doctor can receive one loan only under this scheme.
- The loans will be available from 1 July 2027 through the existing Small Business Cashflow Loan Scheme.
- Corporate-owned practices are excluded.

##### Example: How it benefits your local community

Katherine wants to move back to her hometown of Cambridge to buy a house and be closer to her family. A local doctor in Cambridge is retiring and wants to sell his practice in 2029. He has had interest from a corporate provider but would like the practice to remain owner-operated. Katherine would need to borrow $400,000 to buy into the practice and could be paying back upwards of $5,000 a month if borrowing through a bank. She is reluctant to take on this loan which would be on top of a planned $500,000 mortgage with monthly repayments of $2,500.

With Labour's Family Doctor Loan Scheme, she would be able to borrow the $400,000 to buy into the practice. If approved, she would have no repayments and no interest until 2031, and then until 2039 to pay off the loan. This reduces the risk for Katherine and lets her spend the first two years focusing on patients and ensuring the clinic runs smoothly, rather than worrying about monthly payments.

### Why this is needed

Family doctors are the backbone of our health system and the first port of call when people are unwell - taking pressure off our busy hospitals. But doctors tell us that owning a practice is not always a sustainable option, especially for younger GPs with student loans, starting families, or trying to buy their first home.

Right now under Christopher Luxon, it is getting harder and more expensive to see a doctor or nurse in your community. Currently, 650,000 people cannot afford to see a doctor. One in three people are waiting more than two weeks for an appointment, and more than one in six are waiting three or four weeks, or longer. Around 300,000 people are not enrolled with a practice, and in some places very few practices are open for new enrolments.

“As a frontline ambulance officer, I often feel overwhelmed by how sick people are getting because they cannot get a GP appointment when it is needed or cannot afford the cost.”

### How Labour will free up 4.5 million GP appointments a year

Labour has worked with health experts on a practical plan to free up more than 4.5 million GP appointments every year - simple, affordable changes that free up doctors' time so they can focus on patients, not paperwork.

Simple, affordable changes that free up doctors' time so they can focus on patients.

| Change | Appointments freed up per year |
| --- | --- |
| Clinical phone triage, directing patients to the right care | ~1.9 million (plus a further 2.9 million visits streamlined) |
| Expanding the use of technology to reduce administration | ~1.5 million |
| Support for advice on long-term conditions | ~1 million |
| Targeted funding to expand clinic space in high-demand areas | ~180,000 |

Where a patient's issue is resolved through telehealth triage, it will not count against their annual entitlement to three free doctor's visits.

#### Other changes in the plan

- A new Digital Innovation Fund, so clinics can quickly trial and adopt the best new technology as it becomes available.
- More open and efficient procurement for doctors, including access to the national Health System Catalogue, to reduce everyday running costs.
- A review of telehealth funding to ensure it complements, not replaces, face-to-face care.

### Fixing GP funding

Labour will introduce independent pricing - a fair, transparent funding system where an Independent Pricing Authority sets a national GP funding rate based on real costs and patient need. When that rate goes up, Health NZ will fund the increase, instead of leaving practices or patients to carry the cost. Money that currently comes from patient co-payments will go into general practice funding, so clinics aren't worse off.

### The cost

The administrative costs for the Family Doctor Loan Scheme will be met from existing baselines, as it leverages the existing Small Business Cashflow Loan Scheme. If fully subscribed, the capital cost of the loans themselves would be $25 million a year. The cost to government is the forgone interest from the low interest rate - estimated at less than $8 million a year if fully subscribed.

Frequently asked questions
How much can doctors borrow, and what's the cap?
Up to 90% of the cost of buying into a practice, capped at $500,000.

Who can apply for a loan?
Owner-operated general practices, not corporate-owned practices, with priority given to areas with no GPs or with closed or partially closed books. Each doctor can receive one loan only.

What are the loan terms?
Interest-free for the first two years; a 3% annual interest rate applies after that on the outstanding balance; 10 years in total to repay; delivered through the existing Small Business Cashflow Loan Scheme from 1 July 2027.

How many loans will be available each year?
Up to 50.

How many GP appointments will this free up?
More than 4.5 million a year, through a combination of clinical phone triage, reduced administration, support for long-term conditions, and expanded clinic space.

What will the scheme cost the Government?
If fully subscribed, $25 million a year would be loaned out in total, with the true fiscal cost, the interest the Government forgoes, estimated at less than $8 million a year.

The Family Doctor Loan Scheme is part of Labour's plan to make it easier to get an appointment.

## Labour's $20 Public Transport Fare Cap

From 1 July 2027, Labour will cap weekly public transport fares at $20 in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and at $10 everywhere else in New Zealand.

Key facts
- Weekly fare cap: $20 in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch
- Weekly fare cap: $10 everywhere else in New Zealand
- In place by 1 July 2027
- Once the cap is reached, the rest of that week's trips are free
- Average saving: around $25 a week, over $1,200 a year, varying by region and how far you travel
- No new card, paperwork or sign-up required

### How it works

Just use your public transport card or payment method as normal. The system will automatically track your spending over a seven-day period, and once you reach the weekly cap, you stop being charged. Every trip for the rest of the week is free.

No catches. No paperwork. No complicated rules. Just savings.

### What the fare cap covers

The fare cap covers all buses and trains across the country, as well as some ferries in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch.

It does not cover interregional or scenic trains, commercial interregional transport, or any other ferries.

### How much you'll save, by region

Average weekly savings for a commuter in each region:

| Region | Average weekly saving |
| --- | --- |
| Auckland | $30 |
| Wellington | $25 |
| Invercargill | $25 |
| Napier | $24 |
| Palmerston North / Whanganui | $33 |
| Hamilton (inner suburbs) | $14 |
| Christchurch | $10 |
| Dunedin | $15 |
| Queenstown | $15 |
| Rotorua | $15 |
| Taranaki | $15 |
| Nelson | $12 |
| Gisborne | $11 |

Note: these are average weekly savings. Actual savings will vary by route and how often someone travels.

### Why Labour is doing this

National promised to fix the cost of living. They've made it worse. Under their watch, fares have increased and they've made catching the bus or train more expensive.

Labour's $20 public transport fare cap will get you where you're going for less - putting real money back in your pocket every single week.

Frequently asked questions
How is the fare cap paid for?
Labour's $20 public transport fare cap will be paid for responsibly with a small contribution from an existing fund set up to support New Zealand's transport network. It's a smart, targeted investment that delivers immediate savings, gets more people using public transport, and eases congestion.

When will it be implemented?
The cap will be in place by 1 July 2027. New Zealanders will start saving the moment it is in place.

What will Labour's fare cap cover?
The fare cap covers all buses and trains across the country, as well as some ferries in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch.

It does not cover interregional or scenic trains, commercial interregional transport, or any other ferries.

How much will I save?
It depends on where you live - see the regional breakdown above. On average, people save around $25 a week, or over $1,200 a year.

Do I need a new card or to sign up?
No. Just use your existing public transport card or payment method as normal.

Our $20 public transport fare cap is just one of the ways life will get better with Labour.

Better jobs. Affordable healthcare. Household bills you can actually pay.
