documents/rnz-labour-commits-to-securing.title: Labour commits to securing first pay equity deal by next Budget | RNZ
documents/rnz-labour-commits-to-securing.text:
29 September 2026, 6:51pm

## Labour commits to securing first pay equity deal by next Budget

Russell Palmer

Photo credit:RNZ / Nick Monro

While the government is hailing a bigger surplus as evidence its plan is working, not all the numbers are so rosy and the opposition is warning of more cuts to come.

Both major parties will have explaining to do, with spending cuts built into the projections and Labour yet to explain how it will pay for its promises.

The party's Finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds has also added to leader Chris Hipkins' commitment to pass pay equity legislation within 100 days of being elected, promising the first deal - with care and support workers - would be done by her first Budget.

The Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update (Prefu) opened the government's books for the first time since the Budget in May and revealed improved numbers.

However, economists and business groups have warned the improvements mask some deeper challenges.

#### Labour promises pay equity deal done by first Budget

Edmonds pledged the first pay equity deal under the restored legislation would be done by the time of her first Budget.

"That's my commitment," she said.

"I want to be able to settle this by my first Budget for that care and support workers deal, especially because that's what the unions are saying should be done first.

"We might have to do a mini-Budget anyway because of just the other commitments that we might have, but obviously we'll probably have to set up a contingency for it given there is none."

She refused to accept that could impact the government's ability to negotiate.

"No. What's hamstringing is that our working women have less pay in their pocket over the last three years."

She fended off repeated questions about how much the party would set aside for restoring pay equity deals under the previous settings, saying her fiscal plan setting out the contingency funding would be coming "very soon" and the figure would be "sufficient".

RNZ / Nick Monro

Hipkins, speaking in Auckland after a speech to the EMA, said the Prefu was "the verdict" on National's track record with government debt, unemployment, and inflation staying higher for longer, and a return to surplus still forecast later than the update prior to the last election.

Both stood by the modelling for their capital gains tax in spite of weaker house price growth, saying revenue was still expected to be higher than when Labour did the costings.

"We deliberately costed it conservatively," Hipkins said.

#### 'Our plan is working' - National

National leader Christopher Luxon was touting the improved numbers, but also appeared to back off earlier commitments to changing the superannuation eligibility age.

He praised Finance Minister Nicola Willis' "responsible economic management".

"Our plan is genuinely working, it is working. We have been doing the right things from day one, under Nicola's leadership. She's done an exceptionally good job, there is no better finance minister in this country, and she's going to go down as one of the greatest."

However, having previously said the party would campaign on raising the age from 65 at this year's election, he cast doubt on National's ability to secure changes to the superannuation age of eligibility.

Christopher Luxon speaks to media at The Borough Cafe in Tawa on 29 September 2026.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"If we do it, it would need to be in a very slow, considered, you know, giving people lots of advance notice and lots of time, but it also does require a degree of political consensus as well, and that's missing at the moment," he said.

Willis at this year's Budget railed against parties refusing to lift the age, saying they were "prepared to rob everyone in this country under the age of 50 for their own political expediency".

#### 'Hope is this government's plan' - Greens

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick brought back the prime minister's quote that "hope is not a plan" from the beginning of the fuel crisis, levelling it at the coalition.

"Unfortunately today it appears as though hope is this government's plan, as they sit on their hands and refuse to do anything to actually increase our resilience and improve New Zealanders' outlook," she told reporters.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Swarbrick pointed to what she said was a missed opportunity for the government to decarbonise the economy and better prepare the country for price shocks when the Strait of Hormuz initially closed.

The Luxon government had driven fuel inflation higher, she said, pointing at 10 additional risks highlighted by Treasury in the Prefu - particularly $5b in committed but unfunded military spending.

The government had "very clearly" shifted the cost of the economic recovery to New Zealand, she said.

#### 'Vindicated' - Seymour

In Auckland, ACT leader David Seymour said the Prefu had "vindicated" his party's drive for savings.

"We have saved money in this government, but actually nowhere near enough. And as the bond market increases interest rates on government debt all around the world, we are going to have to go further and faster to balance the books with no new taxes."

He reiterated his call for fewer government departments, and reducing the number of public servants to 1 percent of the total population.

"The surplus being promised is two years later than was promised before the last election. To achieve that is going to require major reductions in the number of public servants and government departments, which I think we should do."

RNZ / Nick Monro

He said that could be achieved without affecting nurses, police officers or doctors, and also reiterated his call for fuel taxes to continue rising.

"You've got to collect enough money from your excise tax to pay for the roads. If you're not prepared to do that, you're not being honest."

#### Too early for tax cuts - economist

Independent economist Cameron Bagrie told Checkpoint that after repeated delays on reaching surplus, the Prefu was one of the first reports showing the goalposts a bit closer.

Audio player for "Bigger surplus forecast in pre-election fiscal update" removed for printing

Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics/1653587%2Flabour-commits-to-securing-first-pay-equity-deal-by-next-budget

### Bigger surplus forecast in pre-election fiscal update

Checkpoint

But it all relied on the government making further spending cuts of 2.5 percentage points over four to five years.

"If you strip out New Zealand superannuation and if you strip out interest costs which are going to go up as a share of GDP, then the belt tightening is 2.9 percent of GDP," he said.

With spending on health, defence and education expected to rise as a percentage of GDP, the cuts would have to come from core services, law and order, cultural services or superannuation, he said.

"Yeah... she's running pretty skinny over the next sort of few years."

Willis had at a recent Business NZ conference hinted National might campaign on more income tax cuts, but Bagrie said that should wait.

"Not at the moment ... once we get a little bit of money in the tin, hopefully, yeah, we should be able to tax adjust tax brackets and remove what's called the effect of fiscal drag. But that's tomorrow's story, it's not today's."

He said the jobs data shows the economic recovery is being skewed towards the owners of capital, rather than workers.

documents/safer-online.md.title: Safer Online
documents/safer-online.md.text:
## Safer Online

Under-16s Better Feeds Digital Duty of Care Monitoring Big Tech FAQs
Basic rules for big tech. More choice for you. Better protection for our kids.

Key facts
- No social media accounts for under-16s. Social media companies will be legally responsible for preventing under-16s from having accounts
- Children's privacy protected. Age checks will need appropriate safeguards for personal information
- Legislation within the first 100 days. First reading and select committee within Labour's first 100 days
- A better feed for everyone aged 16 and over. Companies must ask new and existing users how they want their feed to work: personalised recommendations, or only posts from people and accounts you follow, with the option to switch back any time
- A new Digital Duty of Care. Basic legal responsibilities on companies that run online services, with stronger protections for under-18s
- Action on deepfake abuse. Stronger protections against non-consensual sexual images, and powers to take down harmful 'nudify' apps and sites
- An independent digital regulator with powers to enforce safety standards, investigate harmful practices and take action against companies that break the rules

Social media is part of everyday life. It helps us stay connected, share ideas and keep in touch with the people we care about.

But the big technology companies have too much power over what we see and how their platforms work. Their algorithms are designed to keep us scrolling.

At the same time, scams are becoming more sophisticated, fake images and videos are harder to spot, and a lot of parents are worried about what their children are seeing.

You might feel perfectly safe online. But think about someone in your life who might not. A child being bullied, a teenager exposed to harmful content, or an older relative targeted by scammers.

We shouldn't leave people and families to deal with these problems on their own. The companies making money from these platforms should follow some basic rules to keep people safe.

Labour will put basic rules in place for big technology companies, give people more control over their online experience, and strengthen protections against harm.

### No social media for under-16s

Smartphones and social media are one of the parenting challenges of our time. When all their friends are online, saying "not yet" to your kids can be hard.

90%of teenagers reported using social media

62%started using social media aged 10 to 13

2.5hrsaverage social media use a day

32%of teenagers spend at least five hours a day on social media

Source: Public Health Communication Centre Aotearoa.

We set rules to protect children in the physical world. The online world should be no different.

Labour will:

- Ban social media accounts for under-16s. Social media companies will be legally responsible for preventing under-16s from having accounts.
- Protect children's privacy. Age checks will need appropriate safeguards for personal information.
- Take action immediately. We will ensure the legislation has its first reading and goes to select committee within our first 100 days.

Labour is also taking action to help parents get kids off screens by backing more sport and play, setting clearer rules on screen use in schools, and making online-safety tools more accessible.

### A better feed for everyone

When you open social media, algorithms decide what appears in your feed. They're designed to keep you scrolling because the longer you stay, the more money the platforms make.

You might like the recommended content. That's fine. But you should also have the choice to see something different.

Labour will give people more choice over how their social media feeds work. Social media companies will have to ask all new and existing users aged 16 and over how they want their feed to work.

You can choose to keep the personalised recommendations, or switch to seeing only posts from people and accounts you follow. And if you change your mind, you can switch back whenever you want.

The algorithms are designed around what makes the platforms money. We want to give you a choice about what works for you.

### Basic rules to keep people safe online

Banning social media for under-16s is an important step, but it won't solve everything.

Children can still face bullying or come across harmful content on games, apps and AI chatbots. Scammers can use AI to create convincing fake images and videos. And people can have intimate images created or shared without their consent.

At the moment, too much responsibility falls on individuals to protect themselves or deal with the consequences when something goes wrong.

Labour will introduce a new Digital Duty of Care, putting basic legal responsibilities on the companies that run online services. That means:

- Safer platforms for young people. Stronger protections for under-18s against harmful content, bullying and design features that encourage excessive use or damage self-esteem.
- Reducing harm from AI. Stronger protections against deepfake abuse, including non-consensual sexual images, and powers to take down harmful 'nudify' apps and sites.
- Clear responsibilities for companies. Platforms will have to identify risks, show what they are doing to keep people safe and take action when things go wrong.

The aim is to prevent harm in the first place, rather than leaving people to deal with the consequences.

### Making sure the rules are followed

Labour will establish an independent digital regulator to oversee online platforms and make sure they meet their responsibilities.

The watchdog will have powers to enforce safety standards, investigate harmful practices and take action against companies that break the rules.

This builds on the commitment in Labour's AI Action Plan to strengthen protections against online scams, deepfakes and abuse.

Frequently asked questions
What is Labour's Safer Online policy?
Safer Online is Labour's plan to put basic rules in place for big technology companies, give people more control over their online experience, and strengthen protections against harm. It includes:

- Banning social media accounts for under-16s
- Giving users a choice over how their feed works
- A new Digital Duty of Care on companies that run online services
- An independent digital regulator to enforce the rules

Why is Labour doing this?
Big technology companies have too much power over what we see and how their platforms work, and that their algorithms are designed to keep us scrolling.

At the same time, scams are becoming more sophisticated, fake images and videos are harder to spot, and many parents are worried about what their children are seeing.

We believe families shouldn't be left to deal with these problems on their own, and that the companies making money from these platforms should follow some basic rules to keep people safe.

How will the under-16s social media ban work?
Social media companies will be legally responsible for preventing under-16s from having accounts. Age checks will need appropriate safeguards for personal information, to protect children's privacy.

When will the legislation be introduced?
Labour will ensure the legislation has its first reading and goes to select committee within its first 100 days in office.

How will the "better feed" choice work?
Social media companies will have to ask all new and existing users aged 16 and over how they want their feed to work. You can choose to keep the personalised recommendations, or switch to seeing only posts from people and accounts you follow, and you can switch back whenever you want.

What is the Digital Duty of Care?
The Digital Duty of Care is a new set of basic legal responsibilities on the companies that run online services. The aim is to prevent harm in the first place, rather than leaving people to deal with the consequences. Platforms will have to identify risks, show what they are doing to keep people safe, and take action when things go wrong.

What protections will there be for young people online?
The Digital Duty of Care will bring stronger protections for under-18s against harmful content, bullying, and design features that encourage excessive use or damage self-esteem.

How will Labour tackle deepfakes and 'nudify' apps?
Labour will introduce stronger protections against deepfake abuse, including non-consensual sexual images, and powers to take down harmful 'nudify' apps and sites. This builds on the commitment in Labour's AI Action Plan to strengthen protections against online scams, deepfakes and abuse.

Does the ban cover games, apps and AI chatbots?
The ban applies to social media accounts, however, Labour is also introducing a Digital Duty of Care, putting basic legal responsibilities on the companies that run games, apps and AI chatbot services.

Who will enforce the rules?
Labour will establish an independent digital regulator to oversee online platforms and make sure they meet their responsibilities. The regulator will have powers to enforce safety standards, investigate harmful practices and take action against companies that break the rules.

We want an internet where people can connect, learn and enjoy themselves, with more choice over what they see and better protection when things go wrong.

Social media should work for you. Not the other way around.

## Labour Will Cut The Cost Of Getting Kids Back To School

Monday, 12 October 2026, 11:45 am
Press Release: New Zealand Labour Party

12 October 2026

Labour will cut back-to-school costs for Kiwi families, starting with cheaper school uniforms and more choice about where parents buy them.

“Getting kids ready for school shouldn’t mean starting the term with another big bill. Families are already stretched, and school costs can push household budgets to the limit,” Labour Leader Chris Hipkins said.

“Parents deserve a fair go. We’ll cut the cost of school uniforms, bring back healthy school lunches and work towards restoring rural school buses, taking pressure off family budgets.

“Cost should never be a barrier to a good education. We’re focused on making life more affordable for families.

“Labour will make school uniforms cheaper by limiting the number of compulsory branded items schools can require and allowing affordable, generic alternatives that meet uniform requirements.

“Families shouldn’t need to turn to hardship support just to get their kids ready for school. We can take practical steps to bring those costs down,” Chris Hipkins said.

Under Labour, schools will be required to:

- Limit the number of compulsory branded uniform items families must buy.
- Allow affordable, non-branded alternatives that meet school uniform requirements.
- Take affordability into account when setting uniform policies.
- Track and publish uniform costs so progress towards making uniforms cheaper can be measured.

Advertisement - scroll to continue reading

“Schools can maintain their identity without forcing parents to pay a premium for a logo. If a plain navy polo does the job, parents shouldn’t have to pay more for the branded version,” Labour education spokesperson Ginny Andersen said.

“I’ve heard from families who get through Christmas only to face another big bill when school starts. Uniforms, lunches, transport - it all adds up.

“Cheaper uniforms are just one part of our plan. Labour will bring back fresh, locally made school lunches from Term 1 2028 and restore the 43 rural school bus routes National cancelled, where possible, working with communities where routes can no longer be reinstated.

“That means lower costs for families, reliable transport for rural kids and healthy lunches that help children learn.

“Getting an education shouldn’t come with a price tag that puts families under pressure. Labour will make school more affordable for parents and better for kids,” Ginny Andersen said.

## Labour Will Get Kiwis A Better Deal From Banks

Wednesday, 7 October 2026, 12:53 pm
Press Release: New Zealand Labour Party

Labour will open up New Zealand’s banking sector to more competition, giving Kiwis more choice and making the big banks work harder for their business.

“This election is about the cost of living. Almost every Kiwi relies on a bank to get paid, pay the bills, buy a home or grow a business,” Labour Leader Chris Hipkins said.

“Four big banks dominate our banking sector. When there isn’t enough competition, customers have less choice and banks have less reason to offer them a better deal.

“Labour will break down the barriers that stop new competitors taking on the big banks.

“When banks compete harder, Kiwis get more choice and more power to shop around for a better deal,” Chris Hipkins said.

Labour will:

- Give Kiwis more choice: Introduce a new e-money licence for businesses offering services like digital wallets and payments, with rules that reflect what they do and the risks involved.
- Open up the banking system: Make sure smaller providers can access essential banking and payments infrastructure on fair terms.
- Give Kiwis 24/7 access to their money: Require a secure, 24-hour, seven-day-a-week real-time payments system by 2030.
- Back new competitors: Create a clearer pathway for innovative financial providers to grow into genuine banking competitors.
- Make it easier to switch: Make government-verified identity easier to use across banks and fintechs, reducing the hassle of signing up or switching.

Advertisement - scroll to continue reading

“The big four banks hold around 85 to 90 percent of registered bank assets. For most Kiwis, that means too few real choices about who they bank with and what services they use,” Labour Commerce spokesperson Arena Williams said.

“Technology has changed what’s possible. You shouldn’t have to rely on one of the big banks for every financial service you use, and new providers with a better offer should have a fair chance to win your business.

“Labour will make it easier for new providers to get started, grow and access the systems they need to compete. If the big banks won’t provide fair access, we’ll step in.

“We’ll modernise our payments system too. Kiwis should be able to move their own money when they need to, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and if you find a better deal switching providers shouldn’t be a hassle.

“Kiwibank has an important role too. Labour created it and we’ll keep it 100 percent New Zealand-owned. But one challenger isn’t enough – Kiwis deserve more competition and more choice across banking.

“National promised to shake up banking but three years later, the big four are still calling the shots.

“Labour will open up the system, bring in new competition and give Kiwis more power to choose,” Arena Williams said.

documents/scoop-labours-first-budget-pay.title: Labour’s First-Budget Pay Equity Pledge Offers Historic Step For 65,000 Care And Support Workers
documents/scoop-labours-first-budget-pay.text:
## Labour’s First-Budget Pay Equity Pledge Offers Historic Step For 65,000 Care And Support Workers

Wednesday, 30 September 2026, 9:50 am
Press Release: E Tu

E tū welcomes Labour finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds’ commitment to settle the care and support workers’ pay equity claim by her first Budget, saying delivery would mark a historic advance for 65,000 workers and their families.

The pledge builds on Labour leader Chris Hipkins’ commitment to pass legislation restoring pay equity within 100 days of taking office, with care and support workers first in line for a settlement.

E tū National Secretary Rachel Mackintosh says the commitment recognises the determination of workers who have spent years fighting for their work to be properly valued.

“Barbara Edmonds and Labour have given care and support workers a clear commitment and a deadline. Delivering this settlement by a new Labour government’s first Budget will be a historic achievement for workers who have waited far too long,” Rachel says.

“Care and support workers support older people and disabled people to live with dignity and independence. They bring skill, experience and judgment to work that carries enormous responsibility. Their wages must reflect that.”

The commitment is the latest development in a struggle stretching back decades. Kristine Bartlett’s landmark equal pay case, lodged in 2012 with union backing, challenged the undervaluation of work predominantly done by women. It led to the historic 2017 settlement, lifting wages for tens of thousands of care and support workers.

“Kristine Bartlett and her fellow union members changed lives by standing together and challenging discrimination that had been accepted for generations,” Rachel says.

Advertisement - scroll to continue reading

“The 2017 settlement was a historic victory. Settling the current claim is the next essential step for pay equity, building on that achievement and recognising the value of care and support work today.

“Restoring the legislation within 100 days and completing this settlement by the first Budget would turn a promise of fairness into a concrete result for 65,000 workers.”

E tū home support worker Tamara Baddeley says:

“As one of the thousands of care and support workers who had their pay equity claims scrapped in 2025, it is fantastic to hear Chris Hipkins commit publicly to reinstating the Pay Equity legislation, within Labour’s first 100 days in power.

“This is a huge start, and I look forward to seeing the commitment delivered in our pay packets as quickly as possible.

“I, and all care workers, look forward to the day the care and support worker claim is settled in full, with a comprehensive regular review mechanism built in to the legislation.”

Rachel says fair pay for care and support workers will also benefit communities and the wider economy.

“Care and support workers put money into their communities every payday. They buy groceries, pay for transport, get their cars repaired and support local businesses. Better pay means more security for their families and more money flowing through local economies.

“Their work also helps family members remain in paid employment, knowing their loved ones have the support they need. This workforce makes an enormous contribution to New Zealand.”

E tū says workers and their unions will keep campaigning to ensure the commitment is delivered.

“Our members have kept organising and speaking out through years of delays and setbacks. This commitment reflects their determination and the strength of their case.

“We welcome Labour’s pledge. A new Labour government will have the opportunity to make its first Budget a milestone for pay equity. Care and support workers look forward to seeing that opportunity deliver for them and all our communities.”

documents/scoop-make-it-16-welcomes-labo.title: Make It 16 Welcomes Labour’s Support For 16 And 17 Year-Olds Voting At Local Elections
documents/scoop-make-it-16-welcomes-labo.text:
## Make It 16 Welcomes Labour’s Support For 16 And 17 Year-Olds Voting At Local Elections

Thursday, 1 October 2026, 5:18 pm
Press Release: Make It 16

Make It 16, the youth-led, non-partisan campaign to extend voting rights to 16 and 17-year-olds, is stoked to see Labour’s announcement today on the voting age.

“Following our 2022 Supreme Court win, the last Labour-led Government introduced legislation to extend voting rights to 16 and 17-year-olds for local elections” says 17-year-old Jamin Fountain, Make It 16 Co-Director, “unfortunately that law only got First Reading before the 2023 General Election”.

“It is fantastic that Labour have committed to strengthening New Zealand’s democracy by re-introducing their Bill to Parliament if they form government. We call on a Labour-led government to prioritise making this change in time for the 2028 local elections.”

Make It 16 also acknowledges the support of other parties for lowering the voting age. The Green Party and Te Pāti Māori joined Labour in 2023 voting in support of the First Reading of the Electoral (Lowering Voting Age for Local Elections and Polls) Legislation Bill.

“We have been working hard this year and building momentum and Labour’s announcement gives us even more momentum as we go head first into the upcoming election. We now call on the rest of Aotearoa’s political parties to follow suit and recognise the Supreme Court's ruling that the current voting age is an unjustified breach of New Zealand’s Bill of Rights. Votes at 16 will strengthen our democracy not only for our rangatahi, but for everyone.”

“Ideally all parties would support lowering the voting age for both local and general elections. Because you currently need 75% support of Parliament to change the voting age at general elections, we understand the reason for Labour’s announcement being confined to local elections at this time.”

Advertisement - scroll to continue reading

“In Scotland, once people saw votes at 16 in practice during the independence referendum all Scottish political parties voted in favour of expanding the right to other elections. We strongly believe that once New Zealanders see the positive impact of 16 and 17 year-olds voting in local elections, we will get consensus for general elections too”.

documents/small-business-action-plan.md.title: Labour's Small Business Action Plan
documents/small-business-action-plan.md.text:
## Small Business Action Plan

Under a Labour Government, small business owners will get paid sooner, get more support to invest in the equipment they need, and keep more of what they earn.

Key facts
- Paid on time. Big companies will have to pay small businesses within 15 days for invoices under $25,000 and publish how quickly they pay. Legislation will be introduced within the first 100 days of a Labour Government
- Help to invest. Small businesses will be able to invest up to $10,000 in new equipment and write off the full amount from their tax bill straight away from 1 July 2027. Around 500,000 businesses will be eligible
- Room to grow. No compulsory GST registration until $80,000, from 1 July 2028
- Fully funded by refocusing Investment Boost, costed at $1.56 billion over four years

Running a small business should mean building something of your own, not spending your evenings or weekends chasing overdue invoices and filling in forms.

Under a Labour Government, small business owners will get paid sooner, get more support to invest in the equipment they need, and keep more of what they earn.

We know how hard you work for every dollar. You deserve more time and certainty to grow the business you built.

### Paid on time

You do the work, so you should be paid on time.

Labour will require big businesses to pay small suppliers within 15 days for invoices of $25,000 or less. Legislation will be introduced within the first 100 days of a Labour Government.

Big businesses will also have to publish how quickly they pay invoices, so small businesses know what to expect before they take the work. Labour will do this by restoring the disclosure requirements in the Business Payment Practices Act 2023, also within the first 100 days.

#### If a large business pays late

Small businesses will be able to report late payments to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE). Penalties will be proportionate with repeated late payment likely to result in a bigger fine.

#### Who the rule applies to

A "large business" is one that, in each of the previous two financial years, had revenue above $33 million (excluding GST) and operating expenditure above $10 million, excluding wages, salaries, and payments within the same corporate group.

The rule also applies to the government. Government agencies are already committed to paying 95% of domestic invoices within 10 working days, and Labour says the private sector should meet the same standard.

### Help to invest

Write off investments up to $10,000 from your tax bill straight away, so you keep more in your first year and save time on tax admin.

Small business owners know what their business needs better than any government does. Labour will lift the low-value asset write-off threshold from $1,000 to $10,000 for businesses with annual revenue below $10 million, from 1 July 2027.

That means a tradie buying tools, a cafe replacing an oven or a mechanic upgrading equipment can deduct the full cost in the year they buy it, rather than depreciating it over years. Around 500,000 businesses will be eligible.

The write-off is a timing benefit: businesses receive the deduction immediately rather than over several years. Labour says this improves cash flow and can make the difference between replacing essential equipment now or having to wait.

### Room to grow

No compulsory GST registration until $80,000.

Labour will lift the GST registration threshold from $60,000 to $80,000, starting 1 July 2028.

Crossing the $60,000 threshold means a sudden jump in compliance, and adding an extra 15% on the price you charge your customers. Lifting the threshold means around 35,000 of the smallest businesses will no longer have to add GST to their prices, or file GST returns. Businesses that want to stay registered still can.

The GST threshold has not changed since 1 April 2009, when it rose from $40,000 to $60,000.

### Why it matters

Small business owners take the risk, put in the hours, employ locally and keep their communities running. But too often their money is held up by bigger companies, while paperwork cuts into the time they could spend with customers, finding new work, or getting home to their families.

Christopher Luxon is out of touch with the pressure small businesses are under. At a Rotorua business chamber event, he said that struggling owners were "too negative" and described them as defaulting to a "parent-child" mentality.

Getting paid on time can mean making payroll without the stress. A faster tax deduction can mean replacing broken equipment, or taking on a bigger job. A higher GST threshold can mean less time doing returns, and not having to charge that bit extra to your customers.

Labour understands that small businesses are the backbone of our economy. We will back them, help them grow, and build the economy from the ground up.

### Getting the economy moving

Backing small businesses is part of Labour's plan to get the economy moving. Small businesses make up 97% of all New Zealand businesses. Give them more cash, a better way to invest, and more time, and the whole country benefits. That's what this package does.

#### Cash moving through the economy

When a small business is paid quickly, that money goes straight back to work (wages, stock or the next job). And it flows through the rest of the economy.

#### Better equipment, higher productivity

Lifting the write-off to $10,000 means a business can buy the equipment it needs and claim the full cost that year. Up to 500,000 businesses will be able to make the call on how best to invest in their future.

#### Room to take on more work

A higher GST threshold means a sole trader can grow into bigger jobs instead of stopping short of $60,000 to stay under the line.

More cash circulating. More investment. More work taken on. That's growth from the ground up.

### Fully costed. Fully paid for.

The package will be fully funded by refocusing Investment Boost and directing more support towards small businesses. It's costed at $1.56 billion over four years, of which the asset write-off makes up $1.355 billion.

Labour says Investment Boost is not targeted. It mainly benefits larger companies for investments many would have made anyway. An Inland Revenue survey found that 53% of respondents said it had no effect on their 2025 investment, only 24% reported an increase, and just 7% said the increase was significant. Labour says a more generous write-off targeted at small businesses will provide greater support where cash flow matters most.

Frequently asked questions
How does Labour define a small business?
A business with annual revenue below $10 million.

What counts as a large business under this policy?
A business that, in each of the previous two financial years, had revenue above $33 million (excluding GST) and operating expenditure above $10 million, excluding wages, salaries, and payments within the same corporate group.

When will these changes take effect?
- The paid-on-time legislation and payment-time disclosure requirements: within the first 100 days of a Labour Government
- The $10,000 asset write-off: from 1 July 2027
- The $80,000 GST threshold: from 1 July 2028

Why is a paid-on-time rule necessary?
Small businesses rely on regular income to pay wages, rent, suppliers and other bills. Late payments create stress, weaken cash flow, and can force owners to cut spending or take on debt. Getting paid on time means more certainty and less financial pressure.

How will payment-time disclosure work?
Labour will restore the disclosure requirements in the Business Payment Practices Act 2023. Large businesses will have to publish how quickly they pay small suppliers, so small businesses know what to expect before taking on work.

What happens if a large business pays late?
Small businesses will be able to report late payments to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE). Penalties will be proportionate with repeated late payments likely to result in a bigger fine.

Does the paid-on-time rule apply to government?
Yes. Government agencies are already committed to paying 95% of domestic invoices within 10 working days.

How much will the asset write-off cost?
The asset write-off is forecast to cost $1.355 billion over the forecast period, as part of the wider $1.56 billion, four-year package.

Why set the write-off threshold at $10,000?
It covers many of the common assets small businesses need, including tools, equipment, ovens, computers and machinery, and lifts the current $1,000 threshold tenfold.

Why is Labour replacing Investment Boost with this write-off?
An Inland Revenue survey found 53% of respondents said Investment Boost had no effect on their 2025 investment decisions, with only 24% reporting an increase and just 7% saying the increase was significant. Labour says a more generous write-off targeted at small businesses will provide greater support where cash flow matters most.

Why increase the GST threshold to $80,000?
The GST registration threshold has not changed since 1 April 2009, when it rose from $40,000 to $60,000. Some small businesses hold back from taking on extra work to stay under the threshold. Increasing it to $80,000 means more small businesses can take on extra work without having to worry about adding 15% to their prices or doing extra tax admin.

Will businesses below the new threshold still be able to register for GST?
Yes. GST registration remains voluntary below the threshold, so businesses that benefit from staying registered can choose to do so.

How many businesses will benefit from the higher GST threshold?
Around 35,000 businesses with annual revenue between $60,000 and $80,000 will no longer be required to register for GST.

Our plan will help small businesses get paid faster, invest more easily, and spend less time on tax paperwork.

Labour will grow the economy from the ground up, backing the people who back themselves.

documents/small-business-first.md.title: Labour's Small Business Action Plan
documents/small-business-first.md.text:
## Small Business First

A fair shot at work and less time dealing with government.

Key facts
- A fair shot at government work. A target for 15% of government contracts to go to New Zealand small businesses and start-ups, with large contracts broken into smaller, more accessible jobs
- Tell the government once. Look at ways to make better use of information the government already holds, so small business owners aren’t repeatedly asked for the same details by different government agencies
- Rules that work for small business. Ministers and agencies will have to consider the impact on small businesses before new laws, regulations and procurement rules are approved

Labour's Small Business Action Plan will help owners get paid sooner, invest in what they need and cut paperwork. The next step is to put small businesses first when government contracts are awarded, information is collected, and new rules are made.

Putting small businesses first means making sure the government works for the people doing the hard work.

### A fair shot at government work

The Government buys goods and services from businesses up and down the country - everything from cleaning and catering to uniforms and computer systems. That should create good work for small businesses. But long applications and oversized contracts can cost thousands of dollars to prepare, and shut small businesses out.

Labour will:

- Set a target for 15% of government contracts to go to New Zealand small businesses and start-ups
- Break up big contracts into smaller jobs where it makes sense, so it's easier to bid for work
- Remove needless barriers that shut small firms out

Government work should help New Zealand small businesses grow, not shut them out.

### Tell government once

Small business owners shouldn't have to give the same information to several government agencies.

Labour will look at how government agencies can safely share information where the law allows and make greater use of common identifiers where possible, starting with the New Zealand Business Numbers. Under Labour, small businesses can spend less time giving the same details to different agencies, and more time running their business.

Labour will also task Inland Revenue with reviewing provisional tax, filing requirements and the pile-up of deadlines in January and February. A corner dairy shouldn't have to do the same paperwork as a large company.

### A small business test for new rules

New government rules can create costs for a small business, even when that was never the intention.

A Labour Government will put small businesses first when decisions are made.

Labour will make sure Ministers and agencies will be required to consider what new regulations, procurement rules and other relevant policies will mean for small businesses before they are approved.

For decisions that affect businesses, a Labour Government will consider what they will mean in practice for small businesses - whether that’s someone running a café, working from their own workshop or trying to grow a business.

Small businesses often don’t have the same staff or resources as larger companies to manage compliance and paperwork. Where government rules and processes affect them, small businesses should come first.

Frequently asked questions
What is Small Business First?
Small Business First is Labour's plan to put small businesses first when government contracts are awarded, information is collected, and new rules are made. It follows Labour's Small Business Action Plan, which covers payment times, an asset write-off and the GST threshold.

What is the target for government contracts?
Labour will set a target for 15% of government contracts to go to New Zealand small businesses and start-ups.

How will big government contracts change?
Where it makes sense, large contracts will be broken into smaller lots so a local small business can bid for the parts it can realistically deliver, rather than being shut out by oversized contracts.

What does 'tell government once' mean?
Labour will look at ways government agencies can use information they already hold, so small business owners aren’t repeatedly asked for the same details by different government agencies.

Will Labour review tax paperwork for small businesses?
Yes. Labour will task Inland Revenue with reviewing provisional tax, filing requirements, and the pile-up of deadlines in January and February, so a small business like a corner dairy isn't required to complete the same paperwork as a large company.

What is the small business test for new rules?
Before new regulations, procurement rules or other policies are approved, ministers and agencies will have to consider the effect on small businesses by asking what a new rule (or form) will mean for the person running a cafe or working in their own workshop.

How does this relate to the Small Business Action Plan?
Small Business First is the next step after Labour's Small Business Action Plan. The Action Plan helps small businesses get paid sooner, invest more easily, and spend less time on tax paperwork. Small Business First focuses on how government itself deals with small businesses including the contracts it awards, the information it asks for, and the rules it makes.

A fair shot at work. Less hassle.

Small Business First is part of Labour's plan to grow the economy from the ground up.

documents/solarsaver.md.title: Labour's SolarSaver - Solar Without the Upfront Cost
documents/solarsaver.md.text:
## Solar without the Upfront Cost

Labour's SolarSaver removes the barrier that locks most families out of solar power with Government-backed finance, kickstart subsidies, plug-in options for renters and a community battery fund for neighbourhoods.

Key facts
- Nothing to pay upfront with two new Government-backed, long-term, low-interest finance options repaid from savings on your power bill
- No lock-in: Repay the loan early at any time
- Kickstart subsidy of up to $3,000 for low- and middle-income homeowners and renters
- Plug-in solar panels for renters saving up-to $400 a year and paying for themselves in four to five years
- Fair pay for power you share: Fair time of use rates when you export power to the grid.
- $30 million community battery fund so neighbourhoods share the benefits, with or without panels on their roof
- EECA provides free, independent advice as a one-stop shop to help households with system selection, installer quotes and finance matching
- $160 million fully-funded over four years by repurposing the Government's Gas Security fund

### Why this matters

Power bills are up 20 percent in just two years under Christopher Luxon. Families squeezed hardest by rising bills are locked out of the easiest solution.

Sunshine is the cheapest power there is - the only costly part is the gear. A typical solar and battery system costs around $20,000, which is out of reach for most families.

People with money could always get solar. But the only affordable finance available requires a mortgage and enough equity. SolarSaver changes that by taking care of the upfront cost.

### How SolarSaver works for you

Whatever your situation, SolarSaver has an option for you:

##### If you own your home

Two long-term, low-interest loan options with nothing to pay upfront:

- Lines company loan: borrow through your local lines company to cover the cost of solar and a battery. You repay gradually through your power bill. You own the system from day one.
- Ratepayer Assistance Scheme: a low-interest loan attached to your property, covering solar, batteries and other home electrification like hot water heat pumps. Designed by councils, Local Government New Zealand and Rewiring Aotearoa.

Repayments are set below your power bill savings, so you are better off every month from the start.

##### If you need a hand to get started

A kickstart subsidy of up to $3,000 is available for low- and middle-income households. That is enough to cover a plug-in solar system in full, or to reduce the cost of a rooftop install.

Labour has set aside $77 million for household subsidies over four years.

##### If you rent your home

Labour will fix the regulations so renters can use plug-in solar panels that connect to a normal power point. Everything that converts sunlight into usable electricity is already built in - just plug in and start saving.

A two-panel kit costs around $1,500, saves $300-$400 a year on your power bill, and pays for itself in four to five years. Eligible people who rent can also access the kickstart subsidy to cover the cost.

##### If you don't put panels on your roof

A $30 million community battery fund means neighbourhoods can share the benefits of local solar power whether they have panels or not. Community batteries store power and feed it back when people need it most, at peak times, or when the network goes down.

##### If you are unsure

EECA will provide a free, independent, one-stop shop to help you work out what suits your home, get quotes from accredited installers, match you with the best finance for your situation and set out realistic whole-of-life running costs upfront - so you know exactly what to expect.

### Shared power for whole neighbourhoods

A community battery stores surplus power generated locally during the day and feeds it back to a neighbourhood or group of units in the evening, during a storm, or a power cut. It works like a home battery, but shared across many households at once. Everyone nearby shares the savings, whether they have panels or not, owners and renters alike.

Labour will set up a $30 million fund for community batteries. Councils, iwi, community trusts, charities, and lines companies can all apply, with the Government covering half of each project (up to $200,000 per project). Lines companies can apply to build, own, and operate community batteries in the most energy-vulnerable neighbourhoods, or in areas where a battery can defer a costly network upgrade.

Community batteries are already working in parts of New Zealand:

##### Franklin (Counties Energy)

Local solar and battery sharing is expected to cover 80-90 percent of the energy bills of three family-services organisations, who pass the benefit to the families they support.

##### Te Reureu Valley, Manawatu-Whanganui (Kia Whitingia)

Solar and batteries on marae have cut local power bills by around 20 percent, with energy traded within the community at below-market prices.

##### Greerton, Tauranga (Powerco)

Pole-mounted batteries are topping up supply at peak times, avoiding expensive network upgrades that would otherwise land on everyone's power bill.

### Jobs and skills

SolarSaver isn't just about cheaper power. Every rooftop system and community battery means local jobs for electricians, installers, inspectors and solar technicians, in the regions as much as the cities.

Labour will fund the Tertiary Education Commission to work with industry to grow the solar workforce as installation scales up, including apprenticeships, on-the-job training, re-skilling and micro-credentials leading to secure, well-paid careers. $4 million is set aside for workforce development.

Combined with Labour's expanded Apprenticeship Boost, this builds the workforce New Zealand needs to deliver clean, cheap power to every community - and keeps the money households save circulating in their local economy.

### Proven around the world

SolarSaver draws on approaches already working in other countries:

##### Property-linked Loans: United States

The Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) scheme provides clean energy finance repaid through the property, not a personal loan. PACE has provided billions of dollars of upgrades over more than a decade.

##### Plug-in Solar for Renters: Germany

Around 1.5 million plug-in solar systems are registered, with renters leading the way and a spotless safety record for compliant systems.

##### Community Batteries: Australia

Sydney network Ausgrid's shared neighbourhood batteries are forecast to save eligible customers about AUD $200 a year, panels or not.

### What it costs and where the money comes from

SolarSaver costs $160 million over four years, funded by repurposing the Government's Gas Security of Supply fund - money that has been sitting almost entirely unspent while power bills go up. Labour will put it to work cutting bills instead.

The cost includes:

- $77 million for household subsidies
- $30 million for community batteries
- $22 million for EECA delivery
- a $20 million Crown underwrite for lines company loans
- $7 million to establish the Ratepayer Assistance Scheme
- $4 million for workforce coordination

A Labour government will have EECA support, the subsidy scheme, and the lines company and Ratepayer Assistance Scheme loans up and running within 12 months of taking office.

Frequently asked questions
What is SolarSaver?
SolarSaver is Labour's policy to remove the upfront cost that locks most New Zealand families out of solar power. It provides Government-backed, long-term, low-interest finance so you pay nothing upfront, own the system from day one, and repay the loan from the savings on your power bill. It covers homeowners, renters and whole communities.

Is there anything to pay upfront?
No. SolarSaver provides Government-backed finance with nothing to pay upfront. You own the solar system from day one, and repayments are set below your power bill savings so you are better off every month.

Who is eligible for SolarSaver?
- Homeowners: can access long-term, low-interest loans through their local lines company or the Ratepayer Assistance Scheme.
- Low- and middle-income households (including renters): can receive a kickstart subsidy of up to $3,000.
- Eligible renters: can use safe plug-in solar panels once Labour fixes the regulations and introduces the kickstart subsidies to cover the cost.
- Communities, councils, charities, iwi and lines companies: can apply to the $30 million community battery fund.

What if I'm a renter?
Labour will fix the regulations so renters can safely use plug-in solar panels that connect to a normal power point. Everything that converts sunlight into usable electricity is already built in - just plug in and start saving. A two-panel kit costs around $1,500, saves $300-$400 a year on your power bill, and pays for itself in four to five years. Renters can also access a kickstart subsidy of up to $3,000 to help cover the cost.

Is plug-in solar safe?
Yes. Plug-in solar panels are already widely used overseas, with around 1.5 million systems in Germany alone. Current New Zealand regulations simply haven't kept pace with how the technology has developed, but Labour will fix that.

How do community batteries work?
A community battery stores surplus power generated locally during the day and feeds it back to a neighbourhood or group of units in the evening, during a storm, or a power cut. It works like a home battery, but shared across many households at once.

Who can apply for a community battery?
Councils, iwi, community trusts, charities, and lines companies can apply. Lines companies can apply to build, own, and operate community batteries in the most energy-vulnerable neighbourhoods, or in areas where a battery can defer a costly network upgrade.

What happens if I move house?
The panels, repayments and savings all pass to the new owner - the loan stays with the property, not the person.

There is no lock-in, and you can repay early at any time. Evidence shows homes with solar sell for more.

How is SolarSaver funded and how much does it cost?
SolarSaver is fully funded by repurposing the Government's Gas Security fund - which is almost entirely unspent.

It will cost $160 million over four years, including:

- $77 million for household subsidies
- $30 million for community batteries
- $22 million for EECA delivery
- a $20 million Crown underwrite for lines company loans
- $7 million to establish the Ratepayer Assistance Scheme
- $4 million for workforce coordination

When will SolarSaver be up and running?
Labour will set up the EECA shop front, the subsidy scheme, and have the lines company and Ratepayer Assistance Scheme loans up and running within the first year of government.

SolarSaver removes the upfront cost that shuts most families out of having solar power.

Using SolarSaver pays for itself out of the savings it creates, so you save from the first month, own the asset on your roof, and can rely on homegrown power when storms hit and prices spike.

documents/speech-labour-party-campaign-l.title: Speech: Labour Party Campaign Launch 2026 - Chris Hipkins
documents/speech-labour-party-campaign-l.text:
##### Speech: Labour Party Campaign Launch 2026 - Chris Hipkins

E ngā mana, e ngā reo, e ngā iwi, e rau rangatira mā.

Tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou katoa.

Warm greetings to you all.

This election is about the cost of living.

This election is about your cost of living.

It's about the couple who work full-time and still have to check their bank balance before they go to the supermarket.

The parent who is doing everything right and wants to put something aside for a holiday with the kids.

The tradie filling up the van every week and worrying about the price at the pump.

The small business owner who has kept their team on through the toughest few years they can remember.

This is middle New Zealand.

They get up, go to work, look after their families and do their best.

And right now, far too many of them are working harder than ever and still going backwards.

I won't accept that as the future of New Zealand.

I’ve spoken to so many Kiwi families recently who are doing everything right but still feel like they’re going backwards.

The emergency department nurse who is at breaking point because no matter how many hours they put in, they just can’t keep up.

The tradie who is worried that the apprentice they are working so hard to support plans to move to Australia because they can’t find enough work here.

The parents working multiple jobs, missing out on spending time with their kids, yet still struggling to pay for school camp.

There are hundreds of thousands of families like this right across this country.

They're doing everything right, but they’re not getting ahead.

They’re not after a handout. They just want it to feel like the hard work is worth it.

They are who this election is about. And they are who I'm going to fight for.

In 41 days, you can choose a government that puts people first.

You can choose three free GP visits a year. Or keep watching the cost of seeing your doctor climb.

You can choose fairer prices at the checkout. Or just another review while the supermarket giants keep calling the shots.

You can choose a lower power bill, with solar on your roof and no upfront cost. Or a power bill that's already gone up 20 percent and is still increasing.

You can choose a Prime Minister who will fight to get your costs down.

Or a Prime Minister whose response to rising prices was "cry me a river."

Let me just stop there…

"Cry me a river."

Have you ever heard anything so out of touch from a Prime Minister?

Imagine working hard all week to provide for your family, then being told, when things feel tough, "cry me a river."

It made me so angry… It still does.

Because it wasn't a one-off.

He called people doing it tough "Bottom feeders."

He told small businesses flogging their guts out trying to stay afloat "be adults."

Small business owners. Families trying to get by. Nurses. Tradies.

Is there anyone he hasn't talked down to?

People aren't asking the Prime Minister to feel sorry for them. They're asking him to do his bloody job.

The truth is, Christopher Luxon doesn't get it. He's not fit to be Prime Minister.

And I reckon, deep down, even his own MPs know it.

I've never felt more strongly in my life that the National Party is a risk to the future of this country.

Their only answer is cuts.

That’s it.

Oh… And lying about tax.

It’s bullshit.

National say they just need more time.

More time. More time for what?

More cuts? Even higher prices? More smack talk?

Christopher Luxon promised to fix the cost of living. He's had three years. He’s failed.

And ask yourself this - after three years of National, are you better off?
It costs 21 percent more to see a GP than it did three years ago.

The power bill has gone up 20 percent.

The grocery bill has skyrocketed.

Petrol is well over $3 a litre.

50,000 more people are out of work. Unemployment is at an 11-year high.

That's not a government that needs more time.

It's a government that has run out of ideas, led by a Prime Minister who is out of touch.

More time won't bring your power bill down. It won't get you in to see a doctor. It won't put money back in your pocket.

More time just means more cuts, and more costs.

The hospital with the overcrowded ED? It will get worse with another three years of National.

The time you’re waiting to see a doctor? It gets worse.

The cost of the weekly groceries? It goes up.

The power bill that’s already ridiculously expensive? It goes up.

That’s what more time means.

More cuts, more costs, and more pressure on families who are already doing everything they can.

Three parties. Three leaders. Pulling in three different directions.

Wasting time arguing with themselves about things like te Reo on government letterheads when they should be fixing the real problems you’re facing.

That's what chaos costs you.

Three more years of drift. Three more years of cuts. Three more years of higher costs.

New Zealand can't afford three more years of National.

And I'm going to give everything I’ve got to stop it.

So let me tell you what Labour will do. And I’ll start with the cost of living.

First, the supermarket.

Right now, there are two big groups with far too much power to decide what gets on the shelf and what it costs.

I'm ready to take the supermarket giants on to get you a fairer price.

We'll open up wholesale supply so smaller supermarkets can offer you a better deal at the checkout.

And we'll make price gouging illegal.

If a big company uses its power to rip you off, a Labour Government will make it pay that money back.

We’ll also take on the other bills that hit hardworking, middle New Zealand.

We'll cap public transport fares at $20 a week.

We'll freeze fuel tax for three years.

And we'll help people get solar power without any upfront cost - which will save families around $1,000 a year on their bills.

Then there's healthcare.

When you're sick, or someone you love is sick, you should be able to see a doctor, quickly and affordably.

Labour will give every New Zealander three free GP visits a year.

We’ll make prescriptions free.
And we’ll make it free to get a maternity scan.

That's real money back in your pocket every year.

Now, I know what some of you are thinking.

A free visit to the GP is no good if you can't get an appointment in the first place.

You're right.

So we're going to fix that too.

We'll help more family doctors set up local practices.

We'll free up GPs' time so they spend it with patients instead of on paperwork.

Under Labour, you won't just be able to afford the doctor.

You'll be able to get in to see one.

And…

We'll back the nurses who make our health system work.

In two years, National has added just 54 full-time nurses to our hospitals.

Fifty-four. Across the whole country.

Labour will guarantee every New Zealand trained graduate nurse a job.

The cost of living isn’t just about the prices you pay.

It’s also about whether work pays enough to cover the bills.

Right now, there are 171,000 New Zealanders are out of work.

Since National took office, 20,000 construction jobs have disappeared.

Builders. Sparkies. Plumbers.

Meanwhile, schools need fixing and hospitals need repairs.

Labour will get the work going.

We'll improve more than 2,000 schools, and get the hospital repairs already on the books finished.

And we'll back nearly 30,000 apprentices into work.

Getting the cost of living under control is the fight in front of us.

But this election is also about the kind of country our kids grow up in.

I grew up in the Hutt Valley. It's still home for me and my family, and it's where I'm raising my own kids.

The people I grew up around worked hard and looked out for each other.

They weren't asking for anything extraordinary. A decent job. A home they could afford. A doctor when they needed one.

You could put in a full week's work and pay the bills. And if your kids wanted to stay close to home, there was a future for them here.

That was the deal in this country. And that deal's been broken.

In my lifetime I’ve watched while opportunity in New Zealand has eroded for too many people.

Wealth, power and resources have become more and more concentrated in the hands of fewer and fewer people.

I’ve seen the damage done to the lives of regular everyday Kiwis when the public services we all rely on have been starved of the resources they need to do the job.

Cutting public services and leaving everything to the market has failed too many people, for too long.

Trickle-down economics does not work.

It’s time to turn the page.

Over the last few years, 2,000 people have been leaving New Zealand every single week.

Two thousand. Every week.

Over a year, that's like everyone in Dunedin packing up and heading overseas.

Every year.

Our nurses and teachers. Our sparkies and engineers. Our future.

Young people we've raised and trained.

As a dad, I think about this all the time.

I want my kids to have the chance to build a good life here, just as I did.

If they decide to go overseas, I’ll be heartbroken, of course.

But I’ll understand.

What I don't want is for them to feel that leaving is the only way to get ahead.

And I know I'm not the only parent who worries about that.

I’m determined to give young Kiwis more reason to stay here and make a life for themselves in New Zealand.

So today… I'm announcing that the next Labour Government will cut student debt.

If you've finished your study and you're still paying off a student loan, we'll wipe 10 percent off what you owe on 1 April next year.

And we won't stop there.

If you're studying now, or you start in the future, stay in New Zealand for three years after you finish and we'll wipe 10 percent off your loan.

Because if you study here, work here and contribute here, you should be able to get ahead here.

No one should have to leave New Zealand to build their future. We want you here.

We’ve invested in your education because we believe in what you can do.

We want you to have the chance to use those skills and build your life in this country.

Now.

Almost every day on the campaign trail, someone asks me: "That all sounds good Chris. But where's the money coming from?"

It's a fair question. And you deserve a straight answer.

Governing is about choices.

National chose to waste millions on ferries that are still nowhere near the water, and tax breaks for tobacco companies.

And they're paying for it with cuts to your hospitals and your schools.

I'm making a different choice.

Our plan to fix the health system includes free GP visits, free prescriptions and more appointments.

And will be paid for with a simple, targeted capital gains tax on investment and commercial property.

Not the family home. Not your farm or your business. Not your KiwiSaver.

Nine out of ten New Zealanders won't pay a single cent.

I'd rather ask a small number of people to contribute a little extra than ask thousands of people to put off seeing a doctor until they end up in ED.

And the rest of our plan?

The school and hospital repairs. The apprenticeships. The student loan cut. The help with your bills.

That's paid for too. Every dollar of it.

And you won't have to take my word for it.

In a few weeks, when the government opens the books, we'll publish our numbers in full, for anyone to check.

Public money is your money. We'll only spend it where it makes a real difference in people's lives.

That's the choice. And I'm proud to make it.

And if you elect us, we'll hit the ground running.

From day one, we'll take immediate action on the things that matter most.

Your grocery bill. Your power bill. Your visit to the doctor.

I know people have had enough of stop-start politics.

So where good work is underway, we'll keep it going.

If a school needs fixing, let's fix it.

If a hospital needs repairing, let's get on with it.

If a business is ready to invest, let’s give it some certainty.

People often ask me why I want to be Prime Minister.

I want to be Prime Minister because I want a fair go for Kiwis.

I meet people who have done everything we ask of them.

They work hard. They care for their families. They contribute to their communities.

And lately, it’s become harder and harder for them to get ahead.

I am determined to change that.

I'll get the cost of living under control.

And I'll make sure your hard work is rewarded.

I'll make sure you can get in to see a doctor when you need one.

I'll get tradies back to work.

And I'll lead a Government that will give our kids a reason to build their future right here at home.

That's the job.

Now, to our candidates and volunteers.

You are how we win this.

National will have the big money. The billboards. The attack ads.

But we've got something they'll never have.

We've got you.

Every door you knock on. Every phone call you make. Every leaflet delivered. Every chat at the local market.

It all makes a difference.

It’s how elections are won in this country.

Not by putting up billboards with blatant lies.

On the doorstep.

41 days.

41 days to change this government.

I'm giving this campaign everything I've got.

Will you give it everything you've got?

Are we going to knock on every door?

Are we going to fight every day?

Can we win this election?

Yes we will!

This election is about the cost of living.

Christopher Luxon promised to fix it. He hasn't. And more time won't change that.

Let's change this government and get to work.

Better. Starts. Now.

##### Speech: Labour's foreign policy

Tēnā koutou katoa

Members of the public, diplomatic corp, the media, Parliamentary colleagues, it's a pleasure to address you today. My warm thanks to Diplosphere our hosts and our moderators.

Not quite two days ago Minister Peters, spoke to the foreign policy approach this government has taken.

I’d like to respond, to frame our view of New Zealand’s foreign policy objectives and what we mean when we state that we will be restoring our independent foreign policy.

Before I respond to Minister Peters' comments, can I first recognise his service as Foreign Minister during this term and under prior governments.

We disagree on critical aspects regarding the role New Zealand must play in a fraught world, but not on all aspects of foreign policy, and I want to acknowledge in particular the breadth of his travel and the relationships he has maintained in the Pacific as hallmarks of his time in the role.

The shift from rules to power has created what feels like an interregnum where our old institutions are exposed as no longer fit for purpose and matured multilateral architecture doesn’t yet exist, we are in what has been called by some a monstrous world, but in seeing where we are we must also recognise there is power in an interregnum.

The Minister framed this as the worst international conditions since 1945 but that was also the most creative moment in modern international relations. And lets remember that negotiations on the UN Charter began in Dumbarton Oaks while World War two continued to rage and discussions continued as Peter Fraser travelled to San Francisco to help give shape to the institutions of a new order.

Critical work is done in the in-between.

The drafters of the charter didn’t gift the world an eternal solution to war and that wasn’t their objective. Their objective was to give the world an alternative to war in their time in the face of their challenges. For us – they gave something else - a foothold to lift us through future challenges.

The review mechanism written into the Charter itself. It was intended to spark a review within 10 years. Perhaps before the rules of chapter seven became as brittle as they have. This was always the intention. We are late, and now this work can wait no longer.

Labour will support the development of our multilateral institutions, including reviewing and maturing the UN Charter so its fit for purpose. Labour will support the good work of our multilateral organisations such as the World Health organisation and will adopt the updated WHO health regulations.

Independence is pivotal to New Zealand’s Foreign Policy approach. The Minister argued that independence, is about agency. Suggesting agency is about choosing New Zealand's interests over our identity. Leaving our options open.

I believe our interests and our identity, or by another name, our values are tethered together. Independence means acting in service to both. We can pursue our national interests relentlessly as we have demonstrated in the past when Labour secured a free trade agreement with China in 2008, with the UK in 2022, when we negotiated the EU agreement last term and when we diligently put New Zealands interests first in supporting the India FTA this term.

We can be relentless in this pursuit while also standing up for our values.

New Zealand's silence this term on breaches of the UN charter has been noticed. This Government's silence as one after the other - States recognised Palestine has been noticed.

This Government's silence in failing to stand up a sanctions regime, following the ICJ decision on the ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, continues to be loud. New Zealand's abstentions this term, on the floor of the UN whether it be about the reappointment of the High Commissioner of Human Rights or a vote abstaining on indigenous participation at the UN, have been met with confusion by our colleagues in the international space.

We do not grow our agency if we stand for nothing because that too is a choice that has consequences. We lose our reputation as an honest broker and a consistent champion of international law. Make no mistake, the choice to shrink from the moral challenges we face will diminish our agency not expand it.

The foreign policy toolbox will be in full use under a Labour Government. There is a time for quiet diplomacy and there is a time when quiet diplomacy must bend to moral clarity – that is undeniably the case when the scale of human rights abuses is so stark that it amounts to genocide, to ethnic cleansing. Labour will recognise the State of Palestine. Labour will place economic sanctions on Israel and ensure the NZ Super Fund and ACC divest from holdings on the UN list of companies operating in the occupied territories.

Labour will intervene in support of South Africa’s case at the International Court of Justice in respect of a breach of the Genocide Convention.

In this time of tension, we must also remember there are seeds being planted. International Courts continue to perform with diligence the duty of their statutes, people protest with astonishing courage in defence of their rights, humanitarians place everything on the line in the pursuit of development and peace for all, like-minded countries have begun acting on their desire to revisit creative diplomacy in defining new alliances.

Labour will prioritise growing our relationship with the EU and with Canada and exploring options for the development of those relationships in response to the challenges of todays world and in defence of international law, science and our values.

We will deepen our relationship with ASEAN countries, and develop new market opportunities, including in Africa and South America.

In a world where technology is shifting and removing the offramps toward war, Labour will defend peace. We will advocate for an ICJ advisory opinion on the legality of lethal fully autonomous weapons and support international efforts to ban them.

We will establish clear parliamentary scrutiny if New Zealand joins armed conflicts.

We will strengthen oversight of payloads launched from New Zealand to ensure compliance with the current law.

Labour will contribute to the development of the law that protects the rights of women and girls and advocate for gender apartheid to be recognised in the Crimes Against Humanity Treaty.

We will support those whose moral courage defies their reality by strengthening New Zealand’s advocacy for democracy, peace and human rights, including in Myanmar; and establishing a programme to support human rights defenders, providing a safe haven for those acutely targeted precisely because of their potential to bring about positive change for human rights.

Our relationships with both the US and China are equally important to us as major trading partners. Yet under this Government we have not seen a balanced foreign policy approach.

To the contrary, what we’ve seen is outright racism directed at one partner and felt by the Chinese diaspora here in New Zealand and silence when the US acted in breach of the UN Charter. Lurching between racism and silence does nothing to serve our interests nor our values.

We will lead differently. Always respectfully while continuing to hold our Statehood as our own. We will bring a balanced and mature approach that seeks good relationships with both the great powers in our region, and always works for what's in the interests of New Zealand and our regional partners. We will always look to cooperate where we can but we will disagree where we must.

Our Australian cousins as always remain our closest allies and it was a great privilege to travel to Canberra in July to meet with Minister Wong. Notwithstanding some differences in world view, we share so much. In the Pacific and beyond, as we look for friends and allies to pursue our interests Australia will surely be amongst our closest collaborators.

Finally the Pacific. Our anchor. Our Labour Leader Chris Hipkins, began with reference to the Pacific and I will end with it – because for us our place in the world is anchored in our neighbourhood. Our home.

The Boe and the Ocean of Peace Declarations have both emphasised the importance of Pacific Autonomy in the face of external contest. This will be a priority and front and centre as we host the Pacific Islands Forum in 2027.

The region must not be treated just as a site of great power contest. Labour in government will work with our friends in the region to promote peace and demilitarisation, to build ever-closer relationships, and tackle the challenges of climate change and economic development that are so pressing in the region.

Labour will re-engage strongly in international climate diplomacy and support the global transition away from fossil fuels.

We will work towards a Pacific agreement on climate mitigation, adaptation and displacement and Work specifically with Kiribati and Tuvalu on long-term climate adaptation and resettlement.

Labour will progressively increase overseas development assistance towards 0.7% of GNI as fiscal conditions allow.

We will support closer economic integration across the Pacific and make it easier and cheaper to move money and data across the Pacific.

The foreign policy horizon is uncertain and fraught with undeniable tensions. The challenges ahead will require us to be both agile and principled as we have been before. New Zealand has been at its best, has won friends and opened doors when we’re willing to speak up - for open trade, for collective action on climate, for international law, for multilateral institutions, for peace. Just because those things are under threat, it doesn’t mean we should keep quiet. We must work with friends, old and new to protect them.

Tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa.
