documents/speech-new-zealand-an-independ.text:
##### Speech: New Zealand - an independent voice in the world

Thank you for being here today.

Most New Zealanders don’t spend much time thinking about foreign policy.

And that’s fair enough.

They're thinking about the mortgage, the rent, the grocery bill, and whether their business will have a good year.

But the truth is, foreign policy is increasingly affecting households up and down the country.

A tariff decision in Washington shows up in the price a Waikato farmer gets for her milk.

A shipping disruption half a world away shows up at the supermarket checkout.

A cyclone in the Pacific shows up in the work of our defence force, and in the worry of families here with whānau across the region.

So New Zealanders deserve a clear answer to a simple question: what does their country stand for in the world, and how will it protect their interests?

### A world that won’t go back

The world is more uncertain, more fragmented and more competitive than at any time in recent memory.

The assumptions that have shaped international affairs for the past eighty years are under real strain.

Power is being exercised more openly and trade more transactionally.

The conduct of some of our closest partners has changed in ways few would have predicted a decade ago.

We cannot simply rely on old relationships, old institutions or old assumptions about trade, security and international cooperation.

It is tempting to treat this as a storm to be waited out. That would be a mistake.

We have to deal with the world as it is.

We must be clear about New Zealand's place and what we stand for.

If I were to sum up Labour's vision for foreign policy in three words, it would be this:

Independent. Principled. Unafraid.

### An independent voice

Our independence does not mean isolation. It means having the confidence to make our own decisions, in our own interests, and to explain them to our friends.

Generations of New Zealanders grew up with the moments that define that tradition.

There was the Kirk Government sending a frigate into the Mururoa test zone, and taking France to the International Court of Justice.

We were a country of barely three million people, taking on a nuclear power.

There was our stand against apartheid.

And there was David Lange at the Oxford Union, making the case that nuclear weapons are morally indefensible.

None of those decisions came without a cost, and each one tested a friendship. Each one also told the world something true about who we are.

We will never shape events through raw power. Our influence comes from something else: our credibility, our consistency, and our willingness to say what we think.

In practice, that means:

We can trade with a country while disagreeing with it.

We can work with a partner on one issue and challenge them on another.

We can have close friends without outsourcing our judgement to them.

Not independence from the world, but independence within the world.

And as the world shifts, so may the circle of countries we find ourselves standing alongside.

Our partners of the future will be those who share our principles and act on them. We should be open to finding them in new places.

### The Pacific is our home

But our most important relationships are those nearest to us, with our Pacific neighbours and our friends across the Tasman in Australia.

The Pacific is not simply a region of strategic interest - we are a Pacific country.

The Pacific is our home. Our neighbours are our partners, our friends and our whānau.

The challenges we share can only be met together. They include climate change, economic resilience, disaster response, development and security.

Meeting them means respecting the sovereignty and leadership of Pacific nations. It means listening to what they tell us they need, rather than deciding for them.

Our vision is a Pacific that is peaceful, resilient and prosperous.

We want a Pacific that is not militarised, and one whose future is not dictated by rising seas and worsening storms.

We want a Pacific where every nation is free to make its own choices.

That requires New Zealand to be present, reliable and steadfast: the partner that turns up, and keeps turning up.

Australia is central to that. Ours is one of the closest relationships any two countries share.

It is a mature friendship. We don't always agree, and we don't need to.

I want to deepen it further, while each of us keeps our own voice.

### More markets, higher value

As a country of five million people at the bottom of the world, trade has an enormous impact on the daily lives of New Zealanders – it is how we make our living.

But we have to be honest about the moment. Across much of the world, public support for globalisation is fading.

Many people have watched the gains flow to a few while their own work became less secure.

Some governments have responded by reaching for tariffs and turning trade into a tool of pressure.

New Zealand's answer cannot be to retreat, or to pretend nothing has changed.

We must be ready and agile enough to find new opportunities in a shifting world. We must be resilient.

First, we need to develop more markets. The more places our exporters can sell, the less exposed we are to any single one.

We will keep pursuing high-quality agreements that open new doors. We will also defend the rules-based trading system that small economies depend on.

Second, we need to make those agreements count. Signing a deal is the start of the job, not the end of it.

Too many small and medium-sized exporters lack the time or resources to use the access we've negotiated.

We will do more to help them through the door, so the gains reach businesses and workers across the country.

Third, we must keep changing what we sell. There are limits to how much milk, meat, timber and fruit our land can produce.

Future growth has to come from things that aren't bound by acres.

That means agritech and agriscience, environmental technology, fintech, software, gaming and the creative industries.

In these sectors ideas travel, and New Zealand already punches above its weight.

We need more markets, better use of them, and higher value in what we sell. That is how trade builds resilience at home, and how it earns back public confidence.

But while our focus on free and fair trade will remain a cornerstone of our approach to foreign policy, Labour also recognises how important it is for New Zealand to build our own economic resilience so we can stand tall on our own two feet.

We cannot continue to outsource vital manufacturing and processing capability at the expense of local industries, leaving us exposed to international shocks and supply chain disruptions.

At a time of huge disruption in the global energy market, our abundance of renewable energy provides a real opportunity to be more independent, more secure, and more competitive.

Trade is vital to New Zealand, but everyone needs to enjoy the benefits. That means maintaining a focus on local jobs, local businesses and local industries.

### Stand up for human rights and international law

The ironic thing about having an independent foreign policy is that we can’t do it alone.

Climate change, pandemics, conflict, migration and technological disruption do not stop at borders.

A small country in a world without international law, human rights, and the institutions that uphold them would have very few options indeed.

We are committed to the Paris Agreement, the Antarctic Treaty, and scientific cooperation.

The UN, the WTO, the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court aren’t perfect.

But imperfection is a reason to reform them, not to abandon them.

We should continue advocating for stronger and more effective institutions.

But we must be realistic.

Multilateral institutions alone cannot deliver everything we need in the current environment.

That means deepening bilateral relationships, and building stronger partnerships with like-minded countries that are emerging as the world changes.

We can strengthen and revitalise our relationships with traditional partners such as the UK, Canada and the EU, while developing our more recent ones with Japan, South Korea and India.

The future belongs increasingly to coalitions working together to solve practical problems and New Zealand should be active in building them.

Above all, we must apply our values consistently.

Human rights do not become less important depending on who is violating them.

International law does not change depending on whether we are friend or foe.

If we believe in the rules, we have to believe in them when it’s difficult.

That consistency is credibility, and for a small country, credibility is among our greatest assets.

It is why New Zealand has long been trusted as an honest broker.

We have championed small states, disarmament, open trade and climate justice, and we said no to the invasion of Iraq.

That reputation has opened doors and served us well.

My government will restore it as a defining feature of how New Zealand engages with the world.

### Security in a harder world

Can New Zealand keep itself safe in a harder world, and remain independent and nuclear-free while doing so?

I believe it can. But only if we are clear-eyed about the threats, and disciplined about how we meet them.

That starts with purpose. Our defence force exists first and foremost to defend New Zealand and our interests in the region.

It protects a vast maritime domain and supports our Pacific neighbours. It responds when disaster strikes.

It also lets us contribute further afield when our values and interests require it, as it has in helping to train Ukrainian soldiers.

Investment should follow purpose, not the other way around.

The question is not how much we spend in the abstract.

It is what capabilities we genuinely need to keep New Zealand and our region secure over the decades these investments will last.

That answer is changing fast. Drones, cyber, artificial intelligence and space-based systems are transforming both how security is threatened and how it is defended.

We should test every major decision against that reality.

We should also be willing to ask whether traditional platforms remain the best fit for a country of our size, in our region.

Wherever possible, that investment should build capability here at home, in our own industries, skills and supply chains.

But the best conflict is the one that never begins.

Diplomacy, peacebuilding, arms control and disarmament are not the soft end of security. They are among its most effective tools.

Our nuclear-free status remains part of who we are.

We will keep advocating for disarmament, non-proliferation and a nuclear-free Pacific.

I have said that a New Zealand I lead will not join AUKUS, because I do not believe it is in our interests.

But we will work with partners on the new frontiers of security, including artificial intelligence in weaponry and the militarisation of space.

This is not naïveté. For a country like ours, diplomacy, resilience and strong partnerships are the foundation to our security.

### US and China

And we cannot be naïve to the shifting dynamics between two of the biggest powers in the world: China and the US.

The United States is one of our most important partners.

China is one of our most important partners.

New Zealand's interests are best served by maintaining positive, respectful relationships with both, while retaining the freedom to disagree with either or both when our values or interests require it.

I reject the idea that countries like New Zealand must choose between one relationship and another.

That is not independence and it is not in New Zealand's interests.

### Speaking up

But New Zealand has never been at its best when it stayed quiet. So let me be clear about where we stand.

We will continue to support Ukraine in defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

We will advocate for the peaceful resolution of conflicts and disputes.

We believe the time has come for New Zealand to recognise the State of Palestine.

We will continue to speak out against violations of international law, including those committed by the Israeli Government.

We will uphold human rights consistently, without fear or favour.

We will support humanitarian relief and the agencies that deliver it.

And we will back international law and its institutions, including the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court.

For small countries, a world governed by rules will always be better than a world governed by power alone.

### Closing

New Zealand has never succeeded by trying to be something we are not.

Our strength has always come from our independence, our adaptability, our creativity, and our willingness to stand up for what we believe.

The world is changing, and the old assumptions are being tested. But New Zealand's response will not be fear.

It will be a New Zealand that is open to the world and resilient at home.

We will cooperate widely while keeping our national interest at the heart of every decision.

We will open doors for our exporters and build the industries of the future.

We will stand up for international law and human rights.

And we will invest in the peace and security of our home and our neighbourhood.

Our vision is of a New Zealand that doesn't merely navigate a changing world, but thrives in it.

Ngā mihi nui ki a koutou katoa. Thank you.

##### Speech: Trust in Government - Chris Hipkins

Trust in Government
Speech to the Law Association
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins, Leader of the Labour Party

I want to start with what trust in government means around the kitchen table.

For the parent looking at the grocery bill. The small business owner trying to keep the doors open. The young person applying for jobs and wondering whether they have a future here. The family waiting for healthcare.

They hear governments promise that things will get better. But if life keeps getting harder, those promises start to sound empty.

People lose confidence in a government. If it happens often enough, they can lose confidence that changing the government will make any difference.

They stop asking who has the better plan and start asking whether anyone will actually deliver.

That’s a serious challenge for democracy.

People need to see that government can improve their lives. And they need to be able to hold it accountable when it doesn’t.

Today, I want to talk about how we do both.

Why people lose faith

People don’t expect government to solve every problem overnight.

They understand that choices are difficult and resources are limited.

But they are right to expect that when they work hard, they should have a fair shot at getting ahead.

That they can afford the essentials. That healthcare will be there when they need it. That their children will have opportunities in the future.

Right now, too many people are doing everything asked of them and still falling behind.

They work hard. They pay their bills. They try to put something aside. But getting ahead keeps getting harder and harder.

When that happens year after year, people can start to doubt whether the system works for them at all. They lose hope that things can change.

Around the world, we can see the risk when politics becomes a cycle of promises that don’t improve people's lives.

Some people disengage. Others become more receptive to politicians offering easy answers, someone to blame, and the promise that only they can fix it.

Politics becomes a performance. Anger is rewarded. The patient work of solving problems gets pushed aside.

And cynicism can take hold. They are all the same; nothing changes; why bother?

Telling people to have more faith in democracy won’t answer that. We have to give them a reason to believe their vote can make a difference.

An economy that works for people

For too long, there has been too much faith that leaving things to the market would produce the outcomes people need.

That if government stepped back, competition would take care of prices, investment would flow to the right places, and the benefits would reach everyone.

Businesses are essential to our prosperity. They create jobs, develop ideas and invest in our future.

But markets need rules. Competition has to be protected, and customers and suppliers need a fair deal.

When a few large companies hold too much power, the family paying the bill has little power to change the terms. It’s the same for the small supplier trying to get a fair deal.

Telling them to shop around is not much use if their choices are limited.

And telling a community that the market will eventually sort things out is not enough when its jobs are disappearing and its young people are leaving.

Government has a responsibility to act.

That means taking on companies that use their power to shut out competitors or squeeze suppliers.

It means investing in the schools, hospitals and infrastructure our communities need.

And it means helping businesses grow and create good jobs.

People should be able to see a connection between the choice they make at an election and what happens in their lives afterwards.

If they vote for lower costs, better healthcare and more opportunities, they should expect a government to get on with delivering them.

AI and the future of work

We have to apply that same approach to the changes ahead of us.

AI is already changing how people work and how organisations make decisions about our lives.

It certainly has the potential to help us improve public services and make businesses more productive.

But people also want to know what it will mean for their jobs, what happens to their personal information, and who is responsible when something goes wrong.

Those are reasonable questions. Government needs to answer them.

If your job changes, you need a chance to learn new skills. If an automated decision affects your access to a service, you should be able to understand it and challenge it.

And as false information becomes easier to produce and spread, protecting public debate becomes harder. We have to take that seriously.

The benefits of new technology won’t reach everyone automatically.
Government has a role in making sure people have a say in how it is used and a fair chance to benefit.

That also means investing in the places where we build connections with each other.

Strong communities cannot be built online alone.

They are built outside our front doors - in the schools that educate our children, the workplaces that reward our hard work, and the public services we all share.

A secure job, an affordable home and healthcare when you need it give you more than financial security. They give you the confidence to build a future here and be part of your community.

When people can see a future for themselves and their children, they have more reason to believe in the country’s future too.

Delivering change people can feel

For Labour, rebuilding trust starts with easing the pressures people are facing now.

This election is about the cost of living.

People want to know that their hard work will get them ahead.

That was the deal in this country. And that deal's been broken.

Our plan starts with the things that make a difference to a household budget - decent jobs, bills people can afford, and healthcare when they need it.

And we’ll get on with it immediately.

People should not have to wait years to see whether a change of government has made any difference.

We will take on the supermarket giants for fairer grocery prices. That means tackling the barriers that stop competitors growing and giving suppliers a fairer deal.

We will cap public transport fares at $20 a week and freeze fuel tax for three years.

We will give every New Zealander three free GP visits a year.

We will cut eligible student debt, so graduates can finish repaying their loans sooner and keep more of their pay.

And through Start Work Now, we will get work moving on the schools, hospitals and homes that need it, creating work for local firms and jobs for local tradies.

For a family under pressure, lower household bills matters.

So does being able to see a doctor without worrying about the cost, or getting a job that pays enough to cover the essentials.

I am not suggesting that a set of policies will, by itself, repair trust in politics.

We have to earn that trust through delivery, be honest about the choices we make, and answer for the results.

That includes being clear when things are taking longer than we expected, or when we need to change course.

And it means proper scrutiny of how we use the power people give us.
Power accountable to the public

People deserve to know who is influencing decisions. They deserve a chance to be heard before laws are passed.

And they deserve access to the information they need to hold ministers accountable.

Those rights belong to people whether they voted for the government or against it.

When we change the rules for an industry, people should be able to see whose advice we took and why.

When we change a public service, the people who rely on it should have a chance to be heard.

When we fail to deliver what we promised, people should be able to find out what went wrong and demand an explanation.

Our democratic reforms will make it easier to do those things. They must apply to every government, including a government I lead.

Opening up lobbying

First, we will make lobbying more transparent and shut the revolving door between ministerial office and paid lobbying.

People and organisations have every right to make their case to government. The question is whether the public can see who is being paid to influence decisions, and whose interests they represent.

When I was Prime Minister, I asked for work to be done to set out proper lobbying rules. Labour will finish that job.

We will introduce a mandatory code of conduct for paid lobbyists and a public register showing who they are and who is paying them.

We will also introduce a stand-down period, so ministers cannot walk out of Cabinet and straight into a lobbying job.

If someone is being paid to change a minister's mind, the public has a right to know about it.

Access to government should not depend on being able to afford someone with the right connections.

Giving laws proper scrutiny

Second, we will limit the use of urgency.

Everyone in this room knows how much the detail matters – and how important proper scrutiny is to getting it right.

Scrutiny helps Parliament identify mistakes before they become law. It gives people a chance to point out what Parliament may have missed.

Labour will restrict urgency to genuine emergencies, fixing urgent errors in the law, budgets, and implementing a 100-day plan where policies have been clearly signposted before the election.

Every law passed under urgency will also automatically go back to a select committee within six months, so the scrutiny that was missed actually happens.

Governments of both stripes have used urgency too much, including Labour. That’s why we need to change the rules.

Winning an election gives a government a mandate to act. It does not remove the need to listen or to test the detail of what it proposes.

Strengthening access to information

Third, we will modernise the Official Information Act and give it more teeth.

The Act was written for a world of filing cabinets and paper. It needs to work for the way government operates today.

We will codify proactive releases, including ministers' diaries, and create an effective penalties regime for breaches of the Act.

People should be able to see who ministers are meeting and understand how decisions are being made.

Journalists need that information to test what ministers tell them. Communities need it to challenge decisions that affect them. And the public needs it to judge whether government is doing what it promised.

Transparency is not a favour ministers grant when it suits them. It is part of being accountable to the public.

Protecting participation

Fourth, we will protect the right to have your say.

Labour will restore election-day enrolment. Eligible New Zealanders should be able to turn up, enrol and vote.

We will give 16 and 17-year-olds the right to vote in local elections.

We will make it one person, one vote in local elections, ending the rule that allows some people to vote in more than one council area.

And we will require third-party campaigners in local and national elections to disclose donations on the same terms as political parties.

People should be able to participate, and they should be able to see who is funding efforts to influence their vote.

Earning trust

We cannot ask people to trust us simply because we say we have the right intentions.

We have to make their lives better and be prepared to answer for what we do.

For the family around the kitchen table, that means being able to afford the groceries, get healthcare when they need it, and see a future for their children here.

It also means knowing that ministers have to listen, explain their decisions and face scrutiny when things go wrong.

That is the standard I want a Labour government to meet.

People need to see that their vote can change their lives, and know that their voice still counts after the votes have been counted.

If you're not willing to make that happen on behalf of the people of the country you purport to lead, then why be in politics at all?

Thank you.

Stay in the loop by signing up to our mailing list and following us on Facebook, Instagram, and X.

### Speech: Trust in Government - Chris Hipkins

By LabourVoices

01 October 2026

## Start Work Now

What we'll deliver How we'll do it Why the work cannot wait Funding FAQs
Labour will build the homes, improve the schools and repair the hospitals our communities need - creating good jobs, supporting local businesses, and getting Kiwis back on the tools.

Key facts
- More than 2,000 schools will receive funding to improve buildings and grounds
- Health New Zealand's hospital repair backlog will be cleared - only 18 of 152 projects were finished as of 31 March 2026
- Kāinga Ora will get building again plus reliable funding for community housing providers
- Nearly 30,000 apprentices will receive $1,000 towards tools and gear to get started
- Fully funded and ready to start within a year of taking office

This election is about the cost of living. The cost of living is not only about what you pay at the checkout or when you fill up the car. It is also about whether you have a good job and enough money coming in to cover the bills.

That is why good jobs are at the heart of Labour's plan to address the cost of living.

National promised to fix the cost of living. It hasn't. Everything costs more, unemployment has gone up, and well-paid, secure work has become harder to find. Another three years of National means more cuts, fewer jobs and higher prices.

New Zealanders deserve a fair shot: secure work, decent public services and the chance to build a good life close to family.

But right now, 171,000 New Zealanders are out of work. Since National took office, 20,000 people have lost their jobs in construction. Unemployment is now at an 11-year high. Building firms are struggling and skilled Kiwis are leaving the country.

At the same time, homes need building, schools need improving and hospitals need fixing.

Labour will bring those things together. We will get people back on the tools by getting on with the work New Zealand needs. We will also expand Apprenticeship Boost and introduce Māori Trades Training to train more people for skilled jobs in the trades.

We'll create jobs by starting work that has been put off for too long. This is practical work that communities need: building homes, improving classrooms and repairing hospitals.

National has put work on hold while unemployment has gone up. Labour will start the work now.

### What Labour will deliver

#### Better schools

Improvements at more than 2,000 state and integrated schools, with work for local firms in towns and cities across New Zealand.

#### Better hospitals

Long-overdue repairs so hospital buildings are safe, reliable and fit for patients and staff.

#### More social housing

More secure homes for families and more work for builders, electricians, plumbers, engineers and apprentices.

#### More work for local businesses

Useful projects that help local businesses and tradies and create jobs.

#### Back more people to learn a trade

Support more tradies into work and to gain a qualification, so they can earn more.

### How we'll do it

A Labour Government will get essential building and repair work under way quickly. We will focus on the work that needs doing now, not make big promises that take years to start.

#### Homes

- Build more social housing. We'll get Kāinga Ora building again.
- Back community housing providers. We'll provide reliable funding so community providers can plan ahead, alongside a government guarantee that reduces borrowing costs and helps funding go further.

#### Schools

Improve schools across New Zealand. We will provide nearly every school with funding to improve its buildings and grounds, creating work for local builders, electricians, plumbers and other tradespeople.

Schools will be able to improve classrooms, heating, plumbing, drainage, playgrounds and sports facilities. The work will begin in 12 to 24 months, getting people into work quickly.

#### Hospitals

- Clear the hospital repair backlog. We will direct Health New Zealand to finish the remediation projects already on its books.
- Keep hospitals safe and reliable. Once that work is completed, Labour will invest to fix more hospital buildings and essential systems.

#### Apprenticeships

Train the next generation. Apprenticeship Boost and Māori Trades Training will back local businesses to take people on and train them.

Labour will support nearly 30,000 apprentices and provide $1,000 towards the tools and equipment they need to get started.

### National isn't working

Unemployment is at an 11-year high. Under National, 20,000 construction workers have lost their jobs.

National has cancelled, paused and delayed work. Good firms have lost contracts. Tradespeople have lost hours. Young New Zealanders are wondering whether they have a better future in Australia.

But the work that needs doing has not gone away. Delaying it only makes the problems worse and the eventual bill bigger.

We need to stop delaying the work and get on with it.

### Why the work cannot wait

This work is also part of Labour's plan to address the cost of living. It will create good jobs and reliable incomes now, while fixing problems before they become more expensive.

New Zealand needs more homes. Building them gives families security and puts people to work in every part of the country.

A third of school buildings are more than 50 years old. Schools have classrooms, heating, plumbing, playgrounds and other facilities that need attention now.

Health New Zealand looks after about 1,200 buildings with an average age of 47 years. But it spends only around half as much on upkeep as comparable organisations.

At 31 March 2026, only 18 of 152 hospital repair projects had been finished. Another 55 had not moved beyond the early planning stage.

Delaying this work can hit New Zealanders twice. It means fewer jobs and less money coming into households now, followed by a bigger repair bill later.

Putting the work off does not save money. It costs more later and leaves communities with buildings that are not good enough.

### Good work builds strong communities

When a local building firm wins a contract, the benefit spreads.

Tradies get hours. Suppliers receive orders. Apprentices learn a trade. People can cover their bills with a little left over to spend in local shops and businesses.

That is what a good government should do: invest public money carefully, support decent work and leave communities stronger.

Labour will back local firms, give apprentices a start and create good jobs in the communities that need them.

### Fully funded, ready to start in a year

Labour has funded this plan and will use proven ways of getting the work under way. This plan will be funded from future operating and capital allowances.

#### Education package

We will allocate around $450 million to improve the physical environment of New Zealand schools, made up of around $400 million in capital funding for state schools and around $50 million in operating funding for the proprietors of integrated schools, allocated on a similar basis.

#### Health package

We will allocate $200 million in capital for the National Remediation Programme and the Small-Scale Remediation projects.

#### Housing package

We will allocate $2.9 billion of capital for Kāinga Ora to build more state houses. It also allocates $760 million in operating funding to cover the additional Income-Related Rent Subsidy and operating costs for Kāinga Ora and Community Housing Providers.

Labour will invest and get on with the job.

Frequently asked questions
What will Labour build under this policy?
Labour will build more social housing through Kāinga Ora, improve more than 2,000 state and integrated schools, clear the hospital repair backlog, and support nearly 30,000 apprentices into the trades.

How many jobs and apprentices will this create?
Labour will support nearly 30,000 apprentices and provide $1,000 towards the tools and gear they need to get started, alongside creating construction and trades work for local builders, electricians, plumbers, engineers and other tradespeople across housing, schools and hospitals.

What will happen to schools under this policy?
Nearly every school will receive funding to improve its buildings and grounds, including classrooms, heating, plumbing, drainage, playgrounds and sports facilities. Work will begin within 12 to 24 months, and more than 2,000 state and integrated schools will benefit.

What will happen to hospitals under this policy?
Labour will direct Health New Zealand to finish the remediation projects already on its books, clearing the existing repair backlog. Once that work is completed, Labour will invest to fix more hospital buildings and essential systems.

What will happen to housing under this policy?
Labour will get Kāinga Ora building social housing again, and provide reliable, guaranteed funding for community housing providers so they can plan ahead and reduce their borrowing costs.

How much will this cost and how is it funded?
The plan is funded from future operating and capital allowances.

For the education package, we will allocate $450 million to improve the physical environment of New Zealand schools, made up of $400 million in capital funding for state schools and around $50 million in operating funding for the proprietors of integrated schools, allocated on a similar basis.

When will the work start?
Within one year of taking office.

Why does Labour say this work can't wait?
A third of school buildings are more than 50 years old.

Health New Zealand looks after around 1,200 buildings with an average age of 47 years but spends only around half as much on upkeep as comparable organisations. At 31 March 2026, only 18 of 152 hospital repair projects had been finished, and 55 had not moved beyond early planning.

Delaying this work costs more later and leaves communities with buildings that aren't good enough, while also meaning fewer jobs now.

Build homes. Fix schools. Repair hospitals. Get Kiwis back on the tools.

Better starts now.

## Strengthening KiwiSaver for the Future

A better future How it works Fiscal impact FAQs
Labour will create more jobs and strengthen KiwiSaver, so New Zealanders can earn more, save more, and enjoy the retirement they've worked so hard for.

Key facts
- Employer contributions become compulsory from 1 July 2028, including when an employee reduces or pauses their own contributions
- Compulsory employer contributions rise to 6% by 2032
- Employee default contribution set at 4%, with the minimum contribution rate removed for more flexibility
- Bans new total remuneration contracts that absorb employer KiwiSaver contributions into salaries
- A new KiwiSaver contribution for parents while on paid parental leave
- Employer contributions extended to people working beyond 65, from 1 July 2028
- Labour will explore more flexible KiwiSaver options for self-employed New Zealanders

If you work hard, you should be able to get ahead and build a secure future. That's why Labour created KiwiSaver.

KiwiSaver is now helping millions of New Zealanders buy their first home, build a nest egg, and plan for retirement with greater security. KiwiSaver is now worth more than $138 billion and is an important source of investment for New Zealand businesses.

Labour built KiwiSaver, and a Labour Government will strengthen it.

National can't be trusted with New Zealanders' savings. A National Government cut the KiwiSaver government contribution in 2011 and again in 2025, and scrapped the $1,000 kick-start in 2015. New Zealanders can't risk another three years of National.

A Labour Government will strengthen KiwiSaver for the next generation. We will back people to save more throughout their working lives, while making sure they have flexibility when money is tight.

### A better future

Your hard work should pay off, not just in your pay packet and weekly budget, but in the savings you build over your lifetime.

With costs going up, too many New Zealanders are struggling to save for the future. More than a million working-age members aren't contributing to their KiwiSaver, and 83,400 people have had to pause their savings, allowing their employers to stop contributing too and leaving them further behind.

When people can't save, it means they have less financial security, fewer choices, and a tougher retirement. Getting through a tough patch shouldn't stop you from saving for the future. Labour will fix this.

A stronger KiwiSaver will help more New Zealanders:

- Keep saving when household budgets are under pressure
- Build a deposit for their first home
- Plan for the future
- Retire with more security

### How it works

Labour is announcing practical measures to help New Zealanders save for the future. Labour will:

- Make employer contributions compulsory from 1 July 2028, and lift them to 6% by 2032, including when employees reduce or pause their own contributions
- Set the employee default at 4%, remove the minimum contribution rate, and give people more flexibility to adjust their contributions as circumstances change
- Ban new total remuneration contracts that absorb employer KiwiSaver contributions into salaries
- Provide a KiwiSaver contribution for parents while they're on paid parental leave
- Extend employer contributions to people working beyond the age of 65 years from 1 July 2028
- Explore more flexible KiwiSaver options for self-employed New Zealanders

Under a Labour Government, by 2032 most working New Zealanders will have more going into KiwiSaver, helping them plan for the future, buy a first home and retire with greater security. When money is tight, they will also be able to reduce their own contributions without missing out on their employer's contribution.

### Building on KiwiSaver's legacy

KiwiSaver is one of Labour's proudest achievements. When Sir Michael Cullen created it, National voted against it.

Today, KiwiSaver is part of the fabric of New Zealand. It helps people buy their first home and prepare for retirement, while providing a source of investment for New Zealand businesses.

But it doesn't work well for everyone. It works best for people with steady employment who can afford regular contributions.

Only 44% of self-employed people actively contribute to KiwiSaver, compared with 78% of employees. People working beyond 65 can miss out on employer contributions, while most parents on paid parental leave stop contributing to their KiwiSaver. Labour will make KiwiSaver work for more New Zealanders.

### Fiscal impact

Making the employer contribution compulsory and increasing the employer contribution to 6% over time will affect revenue from the Employer Superannuation Contribution Tax (ESCT). This will help fund government contributions to paid parental leave recipients and meet the government's higher costs as an employer, which will be managed through the Budget process.

### Investing in our future

A stronger KiwiSaver means more wealth in Kiwi hands, and more capital invested in our economy.

It will help people plan for the future while backing businesses, creating good jobs and growing our economy.

Labour will phase in these changes carefully, giving people and businesses certainty.

Frequently asked questions
When does compulsory employer contribution start, and how high does it go?
Employer contributions become compulsory from 1 July 2028, including when an employee reduces or pauses their own contributions, and will lift to 6% by 2032.

What is the new employee default contribution rate?
Labour will set the employee default contribution at 4% and remove the minimum contribution rate, giving people more flexibility to adjust their own contributions as their circumstances change.

What are total remuneration contracts, and why is Labour banning new ones?
Total remuneration contracts absorb an employer's KiwiSaver contribution into an employee's overall salary package, rather than paying it on top. Labour will ban new total remuneration contracts of this kind, so employer KiwiSaver contributions are paid in addition to salary.

Will parents get a KiwiSaver contribution while on paid parental leave?
Yes. Labour will provide a KiwiSaver contribution for parents while they are on paid parental leave. Most parents on paid parental leave currently stop contributing to their KiwiSaver.

What changes for people working past the age of 65?
From 1 July 2028, Labour will extend employer contributions to people working beyond the age of 65, who currently can miss out on employer KiwiSaver contributions.

What about self-employed people?
Only 44% of self-employed people actively contribute to KiwiSaver, compared with 78% of employees. Labour will explore more flexible KiwiSaver options for self-employed New Zealanders.

Why is Labour doing this?
Labour created KiwiSaver, which is now worth more than $138 billion and helps New Zealanders buy their first home and save for retirement. National cut the KiwiSaver government contribution in 2011 and again in 2025, and scrapped the $1,000 kick-start in 2015. More than a million working-age members are not currently contributing to KiwiSaver, and 83,400 people have had to pause their savings, which also pauses their employer's contribution. A stronger KiwiSaver will help more New Zealanders keep saving under pressure, build a deposit, and retire with more security.

What is the fiscal impact of these changes?
Making the employer contribution compulsory and increasing it to 6% over time affects revenue from the Employer Superannuation Contribution Tax (ESCT), and will help fund the new government contribution for people on paid parental leave and the government's higher costs as an employer. This will be managed through the Budget process, with changes phased in from 2027/28 to 2030/31.

Backing Kiwis to save and backing the businesses that will grow our economy.

Labour built KiwiSaver and a Labour Government will strengthen it.
